whyWrongByChoice.B: Teratomas are benign in children and, while usually malignant in adults, are not described as the least common or most aggressive subtype.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Spermatocytic tumors make up 1% to 2% of germ cell tumors but are indolent rather than aggressive.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Yolk sac tumor is the most common germ cell tumor of young children and has a good prognosis when localized.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old man is found to have a painless right testicular mass on a routine examination. He has no gynecomastia, no change in libido, and normal serum tumor markers. Orchiectomy shows masses of pale cells, some of which form rounded and elongated structures surrounded by a thick, pink basement membrane resembling seminiferous tubules. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sertoli cell tumor

choices.label: B
choices.text: Leydig cell tumor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Seminoma

choices.label: D
choices.text: Embryonal carcinoma

choices.label: E
choices.text: Testicular lymphoma

explanation.summary: Sertoli cell tumors are hormonally silent masses whose cells recapitulate seminiferous tubule architecture.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sertoli cell tumors are composed of masses of pale cells, with some tumor cells forming rounded or elongated structures surrounded by a thick, pink basement membrane that recapitulates seminiferous tubule architecture. They are usually hormonally silent and present simply as a testicular mass, with most patients being adults averaging 45 years of age. Most are benign, though about 10% behave in a malignant fashion.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Leydig cell tumors are golden brown with polygonal eosinophilic cells and Reinke crystals, and they typically produce hormonal symptoms.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Seminoma shows sheets of glycogen-rich clear cells with a lymphocytic infiltrate rather than tubule-like structures.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Embryonal carcinoma occurs at ages 20 to 30 and shows primitive pleomorphic cells with necrosis and hemorrhage.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Testicular lymphoma affects men over 60, arises from B lymphocytes, and is often bilateral.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man presents with bilateral breast enlargement and a painless testicular mass. Serum testosterone is elevated and beta-hCG is normal. Orchiectomy shows a well-circumscribed, golden-brown intratesticular tumor. Which of the following best explains his gynecomastia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Stimulation of LH and FSH receptors by tumor-derived beta-hCG

choices.label: B
choices.text: Peripheral conversion of excess testosterone to 17-beta-estradiol

choices.label: C
choices.text: Weak stimulation of TSH receptors by a placental glycoprotein

choices.label: D
choices.text: Loss of androgen receptor signaling in peripheral target tissues

choices.label: E
choices.text: Secretion of alpha-fetoprotein by a nonseminomatous tumor component

explanation.summary: Leydig cell tumors overproduce testosterone, and its conversion to 17-beta-estradiol produces gynecomastia.
explanation.whyCorrect: The golden-brown gross appearance and testosterone excess identify a Leydig cell tumor. These tumors produce testosterone and present with symptoms of androgen excess, and patients may also develop symptoms of excess estrogen such as gynecomastia because of conversion of the excess testosterone to 17-beta-estradiol.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gonadotropin-like stimulation by beta-hCG causes gynecomastia in choriocarcinoma, but beta-hCG is normal in this patient.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Weak TSH receptor stimulation by very high beta-hCG explains hyperthyroid symptoms in choriocarcinoma, not this presentation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Loss of androgen receptor signaling describes androgen insensitivity syndrome, a congenital risk factor rather than a tumor effect.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Alpha-fetoprotein is a marker of nonseminomatous germ cell tumors and does not cause breast enlargement.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man is being counseled before orchiectomy and planned adjuvant therapy for a testicular germ cell tumor. He asks what problem he is most likely to face as a consequence of the tumor and its treatment, apart from issues caused by metastases. Which of the following is the most appropriate answer?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Urinary incontinence

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hypercalcemia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Infertility

choices.label: D
choices.text: Primary hypothyroidism

choices.label: E
choices.text: Chronic inguinal hernia

explanation.summary: Infertility is the main complication of a testicular tumor and its treatment.
explanation.whyCorrect: The lecture states that infertility is the main complication of a testicular tumor and its treatment, with other complications relating to tumor metastases. Removing one testis is generally well tolerated because males normally have two testicles, but the tumor and its adjuvant therapies still threaten fertility.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Urinary incontinence is not among the complications the lecture attributes to testicular tumors or their treatment.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hypercalcemia is not described as a complication of testicular tumors in this lecture.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hyperthyroid symptoms can occur with very high beta-hCG in choriocarcinoma, but hypothyroidism is not a described complication.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Inguinal hernia is not listed as a complication of testicular tumors or of radical inguinal orchiectomy here.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man is diagnosed with a nonseminomatous germ cell tumor of the testis. Staging is undertaken to look for distant disease. Which of the following patterns of spread is most characteristic of this tumor category?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lymphatic spread confined to the inguinal lymph nodes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Direct extension across the scrotum into the opposite testis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lymphatic spread limited to the para-aortic lymph nodes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hematogenous spread to lungs, liver, brain, and bone

choices.label: E
choices.text: Seeding of the cerebrospinal fluid without systemic disease

explanation.summary: Nonseminomatous germ cell tumors tend to metastasize hematogenously, commonly to lung, liver, brain, and bone.
explanation.whyCorrect: Malignant testicular tumors may spread by lymphatic or hematogenous routes. Seminomas typically spread first to para-aortic lymph nodes, whereas nonseminomatous tumors often metastasize hematogenously; common metastatic sites include the lungs, liver, brain, and bone. This is why staging includes CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis, and MRI when brain metastasis is suspected.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Inguinal node involvement is an inappropriate pattern that follows scrotal surgery or biopsy disrupting normal lymphatic drainage.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Direct extension into the contralateral testis is not a described route of spread; the uninvolved testis is not disturbed.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Para-aortic nodal spread is the characteristic first step for seminomas rather than for nonseminomatous tumors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: CNS recurrence without systemic disease is a feature associated with testicular lymphoma, not nonseminomatous germ cell tumors.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man undergoing evaluation for a solid intratesticular mass has normal serum AFP and beta-hCG levels, but serum lactate dehydrogenase is elevated. Which of the following best characterizes the significance of this laboratory finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is specific for nonseminomatous germ cell tumors of the testis

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is produced exclusively by syncytiotrophoblasts within the tumor

choices.label: C
choices.text: It becomes elevated only once brain metastases have developed

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is excluded from the staging system used for these tumors

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is a nonspecific marker elevated in about half of testicular tumors

explanation.summary: LDH is a nonspecific tumor marker elevated in roughly half of testicular tumors.
explanation.whyCorrect: Serum tumor markers for testicular germ cell tumors include AFP, beta-hCG, and LDH. The lecture identifies LDH as a nonspecific tumor marker that is elevated in about half of the cases of testicular tumors, so it supports the workup without identifying a subtype.

whyWrongByChoice.A: AFP is the marker tied to nonseminomatous tumors such as yolk sac tumor and embryonal carcinoma; LDH is not subtype specific.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Syncytiotrophoblasts are the source of beta-hCG in choriocarcinoma, not of LDH.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The lecture does not tie LDH elevation to brain metastases; it is elevated in roughly half of cases generally.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The TNM system is specifically modified for testicular tumors to take serum tumor markers, including LDH, into account.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old man undergoes radical inguinal orchiectomy for a testicular mass. Histology shows sheets of cells with pale nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and glycogen-rich cytoplasm with a lymphocytic infiltrate. Preoperative serum AFP was normal, but beta-hCG was mildly elevated. Which of the following best explains the beta-hCG result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A subset of seminomatous germ cell tumors secretes beta-hCG

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any beta-hCG elevation excludes seminoma and indicates choriocarcinoma

choices.label: C
choices.text: The elevation reflects an occult yolk sac component within the tumor

choices.label: D
choices.text: Beta-hCG is a nonspecific marker raised in half of all testicular tumors

choices.label: E
choices.text: The elevation indicates a Leydig cell tumor producing excess testosterone

explanation.summary: Beta-hCG may be elevated in a subset of seminomas, so a modest elevation does not exclude seminoma; AFP is what stays normal.
explanation.whyCorrect: The histology described is seminoma. The lecture teaches that beta-hCG may be elevated in a subset of seminomatous germ cell tumors as well as in several nonseminomatous tumors such as embryonal carcinoma and choriocarcinoma, whereas AFP is elevated in nonseminomatous tumors but not in seminomatous ones. A normal AFP with mildly elevated beta-hCG is therefore fully consistent with seminoma.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Beta-hCG elevation is not exclusive to choriocarcinoma, and the histology here shows no cytotrophoblasts or syncytiotrophoblasts.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A yolk sac component would be expected to raise AFP, which is normal in this patient.
whyWrongByChoice.D: LDH is the nonspecific marker elevated in about half of testicular tumors; beta-hCG is tied to specific tumor types.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Leydig cell tumors produce testosterone and show Reinke crystals in eosinophilic cytoplasm, not the histology described here.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man has undergone radical inguinal orchiectomy for a nonseminomatous germ cell tumor. Imaging shows no nodal or distant disease, and he is being considered for active surveillance. Which of the following pathologic findings in the orchiectomy specimen would most strongly favor more aggressive management instead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A dense lymphocytic infiltrate around the tumor

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lymphatic and vascular invasion by tumor cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Schiller-Duval bodies scattered through the tumor

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reinke crystals within the tumor cell cytoplasm

choices.label: E
choices.text: Granuloma formation at the edge of the tumor

explanation.summary: High-risk microscopic features in localized nonseminomatous tumors include lymphovascular invasion, embryonal carcinoma subtype, and spermatic cord or scrotal involvement.
explanation.whyCorrect: Localized nonseminomatous germ cell tumors can be followed with active surveillance after orchiectomy, but high-risk patients are advised to undergo more aggressive intervention such as chemotherapy or retroperitoneal lymph node dissection. The high-risk features seen under the microscope are embryonal carcinoma subtype, involvement of the spermatic cord or scrotum, and lymphatic or vascular invasion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A lymphocytic infiltrate is a characteristic feature of seminoma histology and is not one of the listed high-risk features.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Schiller-Duval bodies identify a yolk sac component but are not among the stated high-risk criteria.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reinke crystals belong to Leydig cell tumors, which are sex cord stromal tumors usually cured by orchiectomy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Granulomas may occasionally accompany seminoma and do not define high-risk nonseminomatous disease.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man underwent radical inguinal orchiectomy for a mixed nonseminomatous germ cell tumor. Postoperative CT shows extensive bulky retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy, and tumor markers remain elevated. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Active surveillance with repeat imaging

choices.label: B
choices.text: Radiation therapy to the para-aortic nodes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Systemic chemotherapy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Scrotal irradiation of the contralateral testis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Metastasectomy of each involved node

explanation.summary: Nonseminomatous tumors with extensive nodal involvement are treated with systemic chemotherapy rather than surgery alone.
explanation.whyCorrect: For nonseminomatous germ cell tumors, lymph node involvement warrants retroperitoneal lymph node dissection, or chemotherapy if the involvement is extensive. Advanced metastatic germ cell tumors are generally treated with systemic chemotherapy, which is the appropriate choice for bulky retroperitoneal disease with persistently elevated markers.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Surveillance is an option for localized disease after orchiectomy, not for extensive nodal involvement with rising markers.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Radiation to involved nodes is used in seminoma; nonseminomatous nodal disease is managed with node dissection or chemotherapy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Scrotal irradiation is part of testicular lymphoma treatment to reduce contralateral recurrence.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Metastasectomy is the rare intervention reserved for metastatic sex cord stromal tumors, not bulky nonseminomatous nodal disease.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man underwent orchiectomy for a testicular mass that proved to be a diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. Staging shows disease limited to the resected testis. Which of the following is the most appropriate additional management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Observation with serial tumor markers

choices.label: B
choices.text: Retroperitoneal lymph node dissection

choices.label: C
choices.text: Immediate contralateral orchiectomy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Chemotherapy with scrotal irradiation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Radiation to the para-aortic nodes

explanation.summary: Testicular lymphoma is treated after orchiectomy with chemotherapy plus scrotal irradiation to reduce contralateral recurrence.
explanation.whyCorrect: Testicular lymphomas are malignant tumors, and after the initial orchiectomy treatment consists of chemotherapy and scrotal irradiation to reduce the risk of recurrence in the contralateral testicle. Prognosis is relatively good in localized disease, but recurrence, including in the contralateral testis and the central nervous system, is not uncommon.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Observation is appropriate for localized seminoma, not for a malignant lymphoma with a known tendency to recur.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Retroperitoneal lymph node dissection is used in nonseminomatous germ cell tumors, not testicular lymphoma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The contralateral testis is irradiated rather than removed to reduce the risk of recurrence there.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Para-aortic radiation addresses nodal seminoma; it is not the described treatment for testicular lymphoma.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man underwent radical inguinal orchiectomy for a testicular mass, and pathology shows a Leydig cell tumor. Staging imaging demonstrates no nodal or distant disease. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adjuvant systemic combination chemotherapy

choices.label: B
choices.text: Retroperitoneal lymph node dissection

choices.label: C
choices.text: Radiation therapy to the para-aortic nodes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Scrotal irradiation of the contralateral testis

choices.label: E
choices.text: No further therapy beyond the orchiectomy

explanation.summary: Sex cord stromal tumors are usually benign, and the orchiectomy performed for diagnosis is usually sufficient treatment.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sex cord stromal tumors, which comprise Leydig cell and Sertoli cell tumors, arise from neoplastic proliferation of those stromal cells and are usually benign. The lecture states that the orchiectomy done during diagnosis is usually sufficient; metastases are rarely discovered, and resection of those metastases is advised when they occur.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chemotherapy is used for advanced germ cell tumors and for testicular lymphoma, not for a localized benign stromal tumor.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Retroperitoneal lymph node dissection is a management option for nonseminomatous germ cell tumors.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Para-aortic radiation is used for seminoma with nodal involvement, which this patient does not have.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Scrotal irradiation is part of testicular lymphoma management to prevent contralateral recurrence.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man reports 8 months of waking three times nightly to urinate, a weak stream with hesitancy, terminal dribbling, and a sensation of incomplete bladder emptying. Digital rectal examination reveals a smooth, firm, symmetrically enlarged, nontender prostate without nodules. Urinalysis and serum creatinine are normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acute bacterial prostatitis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Benign prostatic hyperplasia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Chronic bacterial prostatitis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Prostatic adenocarcinoma

choices.label: E
choices.text: Acute cystitis

explanation.summary: Obstructive voiding symptoms with a smooth, symmetric, enlarged prostate in an older man indicate BPH.
explanation.whyCorrect: BPH affects about 70% of men over 60 and produces obstructive symptoms (WISE: weak stream, intermittent flow, straining, incomplete emptying) plus nocturia and hesitancy. The smooth, elastic, symmetric prostate without nodules on DRE and a normal urinalysis fit benign hyperplasia compressing the prostatic urethra.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acute bacterial prostatitis presents as a severe UTI with fever, chills, and an exquisitely tender prostate, none of which are present.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Chronic bacterial prostatitis causes recurrent mild UTIs with leukocytes and bacteria on urinalysis; his urinalysis is normal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Prostate cancer is suggested by an irregular or asymmetric gland with nodules, not a smooth symmetric enlargement.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cystitis causes irritative symptoms with an abnormal urinalysis and would not explain the enlarged prostate or obstructive stream.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man has urinary hesitancy, a weak stream, and nocturia. Imaging shows an enlarged prostate compressing the prostatic urethra into a slit-like lumen. Hyperplastic nodules causing this presentation most likely arose in which region of the prostate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anterior fibromuscular stroma

choices.label: B
choices.text: Central zone

choices.label: C
choices.text: Peripheral zone

choices.label: D
choices.text: Transition zone

choices.label: E
choices.text: Prostatic apex

explanation.summary: BPH arises primarily in the transition (periurethral) zone of the prostate.
explanation.whyCorrect: The transition zone surrounds the prostatic urethra as it passes through the central portion of the gland. Hyperplastic nodules in this periurethral region compress the urethra into a slit-like lumen, producing the obstructive voiding symptoms of BPH.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The anterior fibromuscular stroma is not the periurethral region where BPH nodules characteristically develop.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The central zone is not the primary site of benign hyperplastic nodules.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The peripheral zone is not the periurethral site where BPH arises, so nodules there would not compress the urethra this way.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The prostatic apex is not the described site of origin for the hyperplastic nodules of BPH.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia and a 40-cc prostate is started on finasteride. Which of the following best describes the mechanism by which this drug reduces prostatic hyperplasia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blockade of alpha-1 receptors on prostatic smooth muscle

choices.label: B
choices.text: Inhibition of the enzyme converting testosterone to dihydrotestosterone

choices.label: C
choices.text: Direct antagonism of intracellular androgen receptors

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inhibition of phosphodiesterase-5 in vascular smooth muscle

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stimulation of estrogen production to suppress cell growth

explanation.summary: Finasteride inhibits 5-alpha-reductase, blocking conversion of testosterone to DHT and reducing prostatic hyperplasia.
explanation.whyCorrect: DHT, derived from testosterone by 5-alpha-reductase, is the hormone most directly associated with BPH; it binds intracellular androgen receptors and promotes prostatic growth. Finasteride and dutasteride inhibit 5-alpha-reductase, lowering DHT and reducing tissue hyperplasia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alpha-1 blockade is the mechanism of terazosin and tamsulosin, which relax smooth muscle rather than shrink hyperplastic tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Finasteride lowers DHT synthesis; it does not act as a direct androgen receptor antagonist.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Phosphodiesterase-5 inhibition is the mechanism of sildenafil, an erectile dysfunction drug, not of finasteride.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Estrogens appear to tip the balance toward prostatic proliferation, so stimulating them would not treat BPH.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia managed with tamsulosin takes a new medication for erectile dysfunction. One hour later he becomes lightheaded on standing and briefly loses consciousness. His blood pressure is 82/50 mm Hg. Which of the following mechanisms best explains this episode?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Additive vasodilation from alpha-1 blockade plus phosphodiesterase-5 inhibition

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reduced dihydrotestosterone synthesis lowering vascular tone

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reflex bradycardia caused by androgen receptor blockade

choices.label: D
choices.text: Volume depletion from chronic bladder outlet obstruction

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hypersensitivity reaction to alpha-1A-selective agents

explanation.summary: Combining an alpha-1 blocker with a PDE-5 inhibitor such as sildenafil can cause significant hypotension.
explanation.whyCorrect: Alpha-1 blockers relax vascular and prostatic smooth muscle, and PDE-5 inhibitors like sildenafil add further vasodilation. Even uroselective alpha-1A agents such as tamsulosin, which relatively spare vascular receptors, can still produce significant hypotension when combined with a PDE-5 inhibitor.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Tamsulosin does not affect DHT synthesis; that is the mechanism of 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors, and neither drug he took lowers DHT.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neither drug blocks androgen receptors, and the episode reflects vasodilatory hypotension rather than a reflex arrhythmia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Bladder outlet obstruction causes urinary stasis and retention, not acute volume depletion with syncope after a new drug.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This is a predictable pharmacodynamic interaction, not an allergic hypersensitivity reaction.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man has bothersome urinary hesitancy, weak stream, and nocturia from benign prostatic hyperplasia. Transrectal ultrasonography estimates a prostate volume of 45 cc, and his PSA is 2.1 ng/mL. According to current guidelines, which of the following is the most appropriate initial pharmacologic therapy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Tamsulosin monotherapy

choices.label: B
choices.text: Finasteride monotherapy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sildenafil monotherapy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ciprofloxacin for 4-6 weeks

choices.label: E
choices.text: Immediate transurethral resection

explanation.summary: With prostate volume >30 cc and/or PSA >1.5 ng/mL, a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor is indicated rather than alpha-1 blocker monotherapy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Alpha-1 blockers are the usual first-line BPH treatment, but per the 2026 AUA guidelines, a prostate volume greater than 30 cc and/or PSA greater than 1.5 ng/mL calls for 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor monotherapy or combination therapy. This patient exceeds both thresholds, so finasteride is the appropriate choice offered.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alpha-1 blocker monotherapy is first-line only when the prostate is not enlarged beyond 30 cc and PSA is 1.5 ng/mL or less.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sildenafil is a PDE-5 inhibitor for erectile dysfunction and is a hypotension risk with alpha-1 blockers, not a BPH therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Prolonged fluoroquinolone therapy treats chronic bacterial prostatitis, not benign hyperplasia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Surgery such as TURP is reserved for persistent or worsening symptoms or complications after medical therapy, not initial management.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old man with long-standing untreated benign prostatic hyperplasia undergoes renal ultrasonography for mildly elevated creatinine. The study also shows a diffusely thickened bladder wall. Which of the following best explains this bladder finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Detrusor muscle hypertrophy from increased voiding workload

choices.label: B
choices.text: Infiltration of the bladder wall by hyperplastic prostate glands

choices.label: C
choices.text: Chronic bacterial invasion of the bladder muscle

choices.label: D
choices.text: Granulomatous inflammation of the bladder wall

choices.label: E
choices.text: Deposition of prostate-specific antigen in the detrusor

explanation.summary: In BPH the detrusor works harder against outlet obstruction and hypertrophies, seen as a thickened bladder wall.
explanation.whyCorrect: The enlarged prostate compresses the prostatic urethra, so the detrusor muscle must generate more force to empty the bladder. Compensatory detrusor hypertrophy can be detected as an enlarged bladder on exam or a thickened bladder wall on ultrasonography.

whyWrongByChoice.B: BPH is a benign proliferation confined to the prostate; it compresses the urethra rather than invading the bladder wall.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Urinary stasis in BPH raises UTI risk, but the diffuse wall thickening here reflects muscular compensation, not bacterial invasion of muscle.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Granulomatous inflammation relates to granulomatous prostatitis (e.g., after BCG), which involves the prostate, not the bladder wall.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PSA is a protein that leaks into the bloodstream from prostatic epithelium; it does not deposit in the detrusor.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man presents with fever of 39.1 C, chills, burning with urination, urinary frequency, and severe rectal pain. He recently underwent urinary catheterization. Gentle examination reveals an enlarged, extremely tender prostate. Urinalysis shows leukocytes and bacteria. Which of the following organisms is the most likely cause?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Escherichia coli

choices.label: B
choices.text: Staphylococcus aureus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Candida albicans

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mycobacterium tuberculosis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Treponema pallidum

explanation.summary: Acute bacterial prostatitis is caused by the usual UTI organisms, most commonly E. coli.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acute prostatitis arises from retrograde spread of bacteria from the urethra, reflux of infected urine into prostatic ducts, or follows catheterization or biopsy. The responsible organisms are those causing most UTIs: E. coli, Proteus, and Klebsiella, with E. coli most likely.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Staphylococcus aureus is not among the typical UTI organisms described as causing acute prostatitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fungal infection is a cause of granulomatous prostatitis, which shows granulomas on histology, not this acute UTI picture.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tuberculosis causes granulomatous prostatitis, a chronic granulomatous tissue reaction rather than an acute febrile UTI syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Syphilis is not described as a cause of acute bacterial prostatitis; typical uropathogens are responsible.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man has acute bacterial prostatitis with fever, dysuria, and perineal pain. Urinalysis shows leukocytes and bacteria, and a urine culture is pending. In addition to analgesics and stool softeners, which of the following is the most appropriate empiric therapy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Oral ciprofloxacin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Tamsulosin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Finasteride

choices.label: D
choices.text: Warm baths and NSAIDs alone

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transurethral resection of the prostate

explanation.summary: Empiric therapy for acute bacterial prostatitis is a fluoroquinolone or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole while cultures are pending.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acute prostatitis responds to routine antibiotics targeting the cultured bacteria; while culture results are pending, a fluoroquinolone such as ciprofloxacin or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is a good empiric choice. Analgesics and stool softeners help reduce symptoms.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Alpha-1 blockers treat BPH and may help CP/CPPS symptoms, but they do not treat an acute bacterial infection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors reduce prostatic hyperplasia in BPH; they have no role in treating infection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Supportive care alone is the approach for CP/CPPS; a bacterial infection requires antibiotics.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TURP is a surgical treatment for refractory BPH, not therapy for acute prostatitis.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man has had three mild urinary tract infections over the past 6 months with low back pain, dysuria, and perineal discomfort but no fever or chills. Digital rectal examination reveals a soft, spongy, fluid-feeling prostate. Which of the following is the best next diagnostic step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Urine cultures obtained before and after prostatic massage

choices.label: B
choices.text: Transrectal prostate biopsy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Transurethral resection with tissue examination

choices.label: D
choices.text: Serum blood urea nitrogen and creatinine measurement

choices.label: E
choices.text: Repeat PSA measurement in 6 months

explanation.summary: Chronic bacterial prostatitis is diagnosed by comparing urine cultures before and after prostatic massage.
explanation.whyCorrect: Recurrent mild UTIs without systemic symptoms, plus a boggy prostate on exam, suggest chronic bacterial prostatitis. A urine sample is obtained before and after prostatic massage, and the expressed discharge is cultured; a tenfold increase in bacteria in the post-massage specimen supports the diagnosis, though bacteria are cultured in only about 10% of patients.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Biopsy differentiates prostate cancer from benign tissue when PSA is elevated with questionable DRE findings; it is not the test for prostatitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: TURP is a surgical treatment for refractory BPH, not a diagnostic maneuver for chronic prostatitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: BUN and creatinine assess obstructive kidney injury from BPH; they do not identify a chronically infected prostate.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PSA is elevated in all forms of prostatitis, so waiting to repeat it neither confirms nor localizes the infection.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man reports 5 months of pain in the perineum and genitals with intermittent irritative voiding symptoms. Urinalysis shows no white blood cells or bacteria, prostatic fluid obtained after massage shows no bacteria or increased white blood cells, and all cultures are negative. PSA is 3 ng/mL. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Category I acute bacterial prostatitis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Category II chronic bacterial prostatitis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome

choices.label: D
choices.text: Category IV asymptomatic inflammatory prostatitis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Benign prostatic hyperplasia with voiding symptoms

explanation.summary: Chronic pelvic pain for more than 3 months with normal urinalysis and negative cultures defines CP/CPPS.
explanation.whyCorrect: CP/CPPS presents as unexplained chronic pain in the groin, genitals, or perineum lasting more than 3 months, with a normal urinalysis and prostatic fluid showing no bacteria or increased WBCs. It is a diagnosis of exclusion and accounts for about 90% of symptomatic prostatitis. Treatment is supportive with warm baths, NSAIDs, and alpha-1 blockers.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acute bacterial prostatitis presents as a severe febrile UTI with leukocytes and bacteria on urinalysis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chronic bacterial prostatitis causes recurrent UTIs with bacteria demonstrable on post-massage cultures; his studies are negative.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Asymptomatic inflammatory prostatitis has WBCs on urinalysis or seminal fluid but no symptoms; this patient has chronic pain.
whyWrongByChoice.E: BPH causes obstructive voiding symptoms from an enlarged gland, not months of perineal and genital pain with negative studies.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man undergoing infertility evaluation has white blood cells noted on seminal fluid analysis. He has no urinary symptoms or pain. Urinalysis again shows white blood cells, prostatic fluid after massage shows white blood cells without bacteria, and all cultures are negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No therapy; the condition is self-limited

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ciprofloxacin for 4-6 weeks

choices.label: C
choices.text: Tamsulosin with warm baths

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ultrasound-guided prostatic drainage

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transurethral resection of the prostate

explanation.summary: Asymptomatic inflammatory prostatitis is self-limited and requires no therapy.
explanation.whyCorrect: This is type 4 prostatitis: WBCs found incidentally on routine urinalysis or seminal fluid analysis in a patient with no symptoms, with no bacteria in urine or prostatic fluid and negative cultures. No infectious organism is responsible, and the condition is usually self-limited, so no treatment is needed.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Prolonged fluoroquinolone courses treat chronic bacterial prostatitis; there is no bacterial infection here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Alpha-1 blockers and warm baths are supportive measures for CP/CPPS, which requires chronic pain; he is asymptomatic.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Drainage treats a prostatic abscess complicating acute prostatitis, which presents with severe febrile illness.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TURP is the surgical treatment for BPH that has failed medical therapy, not for incidental inflammation.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old man treated with intravesical bacillus Calmette-Guerin for bladder cancer later has an elevated PSA, and a prostate biopsy is performed. Histology shows a mixed, mostly chronic inflammatory infiltrate containing granulomas. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Granulomatous prostatitis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Acute bacterial prostatitis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Chronic bacterial prostatitis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Benign prostatic hyperplasia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome

explanation.summary: Granulomas in the prostate after BCG therapy indicate granulomatous prostatitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Granulomatous prostatitis can be caused by specific infections (tuberculosis, fungi) or by a tissue reaction to non-infectious stimuli such as intravesical BCG treatment for bladder cancer or prior transurethral resection. Histology shows a mixed, mostly chronic inflammatory infiltrate that also contains granulomas, exactly as seen here.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Acute bacterial prostatitis shows an intensely inflamed gland with neutrophils, not granulomas, and presents as a severe febrile UTI.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Chronic bacterial prostatitis shows periglandular lymphocytes and plasma cells without granuloma formation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: BPH shows hyperplastic epithelial glands in stroma, a proliferative rather than granulomatous process.
whyWrongByChoice.E: CP/CPPS is a diagnosis of exclusion defined by chronic pelvic pain with negative studies, not by granulomas on biopsy.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with no urinary complaints has read that prostate enlargement is common with age. He asks whether he should be tested periodically to detect benign prostatic hyperplasia before symptoms begin. Which of the following best explains why routine screening for this condition is not performed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It produces no harm other than urinary symptoms

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is too uncommon in older men to justify testing

choices.label: C
choices.text: No examination or laboratory test can detect it

choices.label: D
choices.text: It regresses spontaneously in most men within a year

choices.label: E
choices.text: Available treatments work only after complications develop

explanation.summary: BPH is not screened for because it causes no harm beyond urinary symptoms, so symptoms themselves prompt evaluation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Screening programs exist for harmful diseases such as cancer. Because BPH causes no harm other than urinary symptoms, there is no need to look for it in asymptomatic men; a patient's symptoms will usually prompt the investigation instead.

whyWrongByChoice.B: BPH is extremely common and increases with age, with about 70% of men over age 60 affected, so rarity is not the reason.
whyWrongByChoice.C: BPH is readily detected on digital rectal examination as a smooth, elastic, symmetric gland, and PSA may be mildly elevated.
whyWrongByChoice.D: BPH is a progressive hyperplastic process that does not spontaneously regress; symptoms may persist or worsen over years.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Most men with early symptomatic BPH are treated effectively with medication long before complications such as kidney injury occur.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old man has had 2 years of progressive urinary straining, hesitancy, and a sensation of incomplete emptying but has not sought care. He is afebrile and urinalysis is normal. Serum blood urea nitrogen is 42 mg/dL and creatinine is 2.6 mg/dL, up from a normal creatinine one year ago. Which of the following best explains his laboratory findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Obstructive acute kidney injury from impaired urine outflow

choices.label: B
choices.text: Volume depletion caused by long-standing nocturia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Direct renal tubular toxicity of dihydrotestosterone

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hyperplastic prostate tissue invading both distal ureters

choices.label: E
choices.text: Glomerular immune complex injury from circulating PSA

explanation.summary: Reduced urine flow from prostatic obstruction can cause obstructive acute kidney injury with rising BUN and creatinine.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hyperplastic nodules in the transition zone compress the prostatic urethra and reduce urine flow. Sustained obstruction backs pressure up the urinary tract and produces obstructive acute kidney injury with impaired renal function, reflected in rising blood urea nitrogen and creatinine concentrations. This is one of the recognized complications of untreated BPH.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Nocturia in BPH reflects obstructed voiding rather than large fluid losses, and prerenal volume depletion is not how BPH injures the kidney.
whyWrongByChoice.C: DHT drives prostatic cellular growth by binding intracellular androgen receptors; it is not described as a renal toxin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: BPH is a benign proliferation that compresses the prostatic urethra; it does not invade ureters the way a malignancy would.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PSA is a prostatic epithelial protein that leaks into blood when gland cells increase; it does not cause glomerular disease.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with a 4-year history of benign prostatic hyperplasia and a large post-void residual volume has had three episodes of Escherichia coli cystitis in the past year. He is afebrile, and the prostate is smoothly enlarged and nontender. Which of the following best explains his recurrent infections?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bacterial growth within urine that stagnates in the bladder

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reflux of infected urine into the prostatic ducts

choices.label: C
choices.text: Granulomatous destruction of the prostatic parenchyma

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neutropenia produced by 5-alpha-reductase inhibition

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hematogenous seeding of the bladder from the prostate

explanation.summary: Incomplete emptying in BPH leaves static urine in which bacteria can grow, raising UTI risk.
explanation.whyCorrect: Urine has a secondary job of flushing debris and waste out of the urinary tract, ideally maintaining a sterile bladder. When the enlarged prostate blocks a strong urine stream, bacteria can begin to grow in the static residual urine, and the risk for urinary tract infection rises.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Reflux of infected urine into prostatic ducts is a route by which acute bacterial prostatitis develops, and he has no fever or prostatic tenderness.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Granulomatous prostatitis follows agents such as tuberculosis, fungi, or intravesical BCG and would not explain recurrent cystitis from urinary stasis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors cause sexual dysfunction, gynecomastia, orthostatic hypotension, and depression, not neutropenia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The mechanism in BPH is stasis of residual urine within the bladder, not bloodstream spread of organisms from the gland.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old man with untreated benign prostatic hyperplasia reports intermittent painless gross hematuria. He remains able to void only small amounts at a time. Urine culture is negative, and noncontrast CT shows two calculi within the bladder and normal upper tracts. Which of the following best accounts for these findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chronic incomplete emptying of the bladder

choices.label: B
choices.text: Prostatic abscess eroding into the bladder

choices.label: C
choices.text: Granulomatous prostatitis after BCG therapy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome

choices.label: E
choices.text: Acute bacterial prostatitis with retention

explanation.summary: Hematuria and bladder or renal stone formation are complications of the incomplete emptying caused by BPH.
explanation.whyCorrect: When prostatic obstruction prevents complete bladder emptying, hematuria and increased formation of renal and/or bladder stones can occur. This patient's small-volume voiding, negative culture, and bladder calculi fit that mechanism directly.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A prostatic abscess complicates acute bacterial prostatitis and presents with a severe febrile illness, not painless hematuria with a negative culture.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Granulomatous prostatitis is a tissue reaction showing granulomas on histology; it is not a cause of bladder calculi.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CP/CPPS is defined by unexplained chronic pelvic pain with normal studies and does not produce stones or gross hematuria.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Acute bacterial prostatitis causes fever, chills, rectal pain, and leukocytes and bacteria on urinalysis, none of which he has.

questions.stem: Androgen signaling does not fully account for the glandular proliferation seen in benign prostatic hyperplasia. Which of the following additional hormones is thought to contribute to its pathogenesis by tipping the balance toward cellular proliferation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Estrogens

choices.label: B
choices.text: Growth hormone

choices.label: C
choices.text: Insulin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Prolactin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Parathyroid hormone

explanation.summary: Beyond testosterone and DHT, estrogens appear to promote BPH by favoring cellular proliferation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Androgens, particularly dihydrotestosterone, are the principal drivers of prostatic hyperplasia. In addition, estrogens appear to contribute to BPH pathogenesis by tipping the balance toward cellular proliferation within the gland.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Growth hormone is not among the hormones implicated in prostatic hyperplasia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Insulin is not described as a contributor to the hyperplastic growth of prostate gland cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Prolactin is not identified as a hormone driving benign prostatic hyperplasia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Parathyroid hormone regulates calcium and phosphate handling and has no role in prostatic hyperplasia.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia begins dutasteride, which lowers the level of the androgen most directly associated with the disease. That androgen promotes prostatic growth by which of the following mechanisms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Binding a surface G protein-coupled receptor to raise cyclic AMP

choices.label: B
choices.text: Binding intracellular androgen receptors to alter gene expression

choices.label: C
choices.text: Activating a receptor tyrosine kinase on the epithelial membrane

choices.label: D
choices.text: Blocking caspase activation to prevent stromal cell apoptosis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Inducing aromatase to raise local estrogen concentrations

explanation.summary: DHT enters prostate cells and binds intracellular androgen receptors, altering gene expression and promoting growth.
explanation.whyCorrect: Dutasteride inhibits 5-alpha-reductase, lowering dihydrotestosterone, the potent anabolic-androgenic steroid derived from testosterone that is most directly associated with BPH. DHT acts by entering the cell and binding intracellular androgen receptors, which alters gene expression and promotes prostatic growth.

whyWrongByChoice.A: DHT is a steroid that acts on intracellular receptors; it does not signal through a surface G protein-coupled receptor and cyclic AMP.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Receptor tyrosine kinase signaling is not the described mechanism of androgen action in the prostate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The effect described is promotion of cellular replication through altered gene expression, not blockade of apoptosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Estrogens do appear to contribute to BPH, but that is a separate influence and not how DHT itself acts on prostate cells.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man whose obstructive urinary symptoms persisted despite 2 years of medical therapy undergoes transurethral resection of the prostate. Grossly, the specimen contains multiple nodules. Which of the following is most likely seen on microscopic examination of the resected tissue?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Proliferation of epithelial glands of variable size within stroma

choices.label: B
choices.text: An intensely inflamed gland with sheets of neutrophils

choices.label: C
choices.text: Periglandular lymphocytes and plasma cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: A mixed chronic inflammatory infiltrate containing granulomas

choices.label: E
choices.text: Diffuse stromal fibrosis without glandular elements

explanation.summary: BPH histology shows hyperplastic epithelial glands, some cystically dilated, proliferating in the background stroma.
explanation.whyCorrect: Grossly the BPH prostate shows multiple hyperplastic nodules that compress the urethra into a slit-like lumen, and its weight often increases 3- to 5-fold or more. Histologically there is a well-circumscribed glandular proliferation of variable sized glands, with focal cystic dilation, set in the background stroma.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Neutrophils in an intensely inflamed gland characterize acute bacterial prostatitis, which presents as a severe febrile UTI.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Periglandular lymphocytes and plasma cells are the infiltrate of chronic bacterial prostatitis, not of benign hyperplasia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Granulomas within a mixed chronic infiltrate define granulomatous prostatitis, seen after BCG therapy or with tuberculosis or fungi.
whyWrongByChoice.E: BPH is defined by proliferation of glandular epithelium; loss of glands with pure fibrosis is not the expected picture.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with obstructive voiding symptoms has a smooth, symmetrically enlarged prostate without nodules on digital rectal examination. Serum creatinine and urinalysis are normal, and PSA is 5.4 ng/mL. Which of the following best explains the elevated PSA value?

choices.label: A
choices.text: More prostatic epithelial cells leaking PSA into the blood

choices.label: B
choices.text: Impaired renal clearance of PSA from obstructive injury

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bacterial destruction of prostatic tissue releasing PSA

choices.label: D
choices.text: Secretion of PSA by the hypertrophied detrusor muscle

choices.label: E
choices.text: Cross-reaction of the assay with dihydrotestosterone

explanation.summary: PSA is made by prostatic epithelial cells, so hyperplasia increases the number of cells leaking it into the bloodstream.
explanation.whyCorrect: PSA is a protein secreted by epithelial cells of the prostate gland. When hyperplasia occurs, there are simply more prostate gland cells leaking PSA into the bloodstream, so the level is often mildly elevated in BPH and commonly remains below 10 ng/mL.

whyWrongByChoice.B: His creatinine is normal, and PSA elevation in BPH reflects increased prostatic cell mass rather than reduced clearance.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Tissue destruction by bacteria describes prostatitis; his urinalysis is normal and he has no infectious symptoms.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The detrusor may hypertrophy in BPH, but PSA comes from prostatic epithelium, not bladder muscle.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PSA is measured as a distinct protein; the elevation is real and reflects the enlarged gland, not assay interference.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man presents with fever, chills, dysuria, and perineal pain, and acute bacterial prostatitis is diagnosed. A PSA drawn during the initial workup is 7.6 ng/mL. Which of the following is the most appropriate interpretation of this value?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is expected in prostatitis and does not by itself indicate cancer

choices.label: B
choices.text: It establishes that a prostatic abscess has already formed

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is diagnostic of prostatic adenocarcinoma at his age

choices.label: D
choices.text: It argues against prostatitis and points instead to hyperplasia

choices.label: E
choices.text: It indicates obstructive kidney injury has already developed

explanation.summary: PSA is elevated in all forms of prostatitis, usually to less than 10 ng/mL, and does not itself diagnose cancer.
explanation.whyCorrect: As in all forms of prostatitis, the PSA level will be elevated in acute bacterial prostatitis, but usually to less than 10 ng/mL, the same range seen in BPH. The value is therefore consistent with his acute infection, and PSA is measured chiefly to exclude the much higher values seen in prostate cancer.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Abscess is suspected from persistent fever and pain despite antibiotics with a fluid collection on imaging, not from a PSA value.
whyWrongByChoice.C: PSA is never diagnostic of cancer on its own; biopsy differentiates malignant from benign tissue when PSA is elevated.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PSA rises in prostatitis as well as BPH, so this value neither supports nor excludes either diagnosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Obstructive kidney injury is detected by rising blood urea nitrogen and creatinine, not by the PSA level.

questions.stem: An 81-year-old man has bothersome nocturia, hesitancy, and a weak stream. He has fallen twice in the past year and has documented orthostatic hypotension. Prostate volume is 24 cc and PSA is 0.9 ng/mL. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial drug therapy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Tamsulosin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Terazosin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Finasteride

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dutasteride

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sildenafil

explanation.summary: For a fall-prone older man with a small gland and low PSA, a uroselective alpha-1A blocker such as tamsulosin is preferred.
explanation.whyCorrect: Alpha-1 blockers are first-line for BPH unless prostate volume exceeds 30 cc and/or PSA exceeds 1.5 ng/mL, and this man is below both thresholds. Alpha-1A-selective agents such as tamsulosin and silodosin relatively spare the vascular alpha-1 receptors that maintain blood pressure, so they cause less systemic vasodilation and orthostatic hypotension, making them particularly useful in older patients at risk for dizziness, syncope, and falls.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Terazosin is not uroselective, so it produces more systemic vasodilation and orthostatic hypotension in a patient who already falls.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors are indicated when the gland exceeds 30 cc and/or PSA exceeds 1.5 ng/mL, and they also cause orthostatic hypotension.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Dutasteride shares both the indication threshold and the orthostatic hypotension risk of other 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sildenafil treats erectile dysfunction and would add vasodilation and hypotension risk rather than relieve obstruction.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man has taken medication for benign prostatic hyperplasia for 9 months. He now reports bilateral breast enlargement and tenderness, reduced libido with difficulty maintaining an erection, and persistently low mood. These adverse effects are most characteristic of which of the following drug classes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors

choices.label: B
choices.text: Alpha-1 adrenergic blockers

choices.label: C
choices.text: Phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fluoroquinolone antibiotics

choices.label: E
choices.text: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole

explanation.summary: Gynecomastia, sexual dysfunction, and depression are the characteristic adverse effects of finasteride and dutasteride.
explanation.whyCorrect: The adverse effects of 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors include orthostatic hypotension, sexual dysfunction such as erectile or ejaculatory dysfunction, gynecomastia, and depression. This triad of breast enlargement, sexual dysfunction, and low mood points to finasteride or dutasteride.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Alpha-1 blockers cause orthostatic hypotension, headache, and dizziness, and may cause ejaculatory dysfunction, but not gynecomastia or depression.
whyWrongByChoice.C: PDE-5 inhibitors are used for erectile dysfunction and are a hypotension risk with alpha-1 blockers; they are not BPH therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fluoroquinolones are used for bacterial prostatitis and are not a treatment for benign hyperplasia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is an antibiotic option for bacterial prostatitis, not a drug given for BPH.

questions.stem: A 73-year-old man has taken tamsulosin and finasteride for 18 months, but his stream has become progressively weaker. In the past 6 months he has had two urinary tract infections and passed a bladder stone, and his creatinine has risen from 1.0 to 1.5 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Transurethral resection of the prostate

choices.label: B
choices.text: Addition of sildenafil to the current regimen

choices.label: C
choices.text: Continuation of current therapy with reassessment in 1 year

choices.label: D
choices.text: A 6-week course of ciprofloxacin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Substitution of silodosin for tamsulosin

explanation.summary: Surgery is indicated when BPH symptoms persist or worsen on medical therapy or when complications develop.
explanation.whyCorrect: If symptoms persist or worsen, or if complications such as kidney injury, stone formation, or frequent UTIs appear, surgery is indicated. Transurethral resection of the prostate, which removes excess prostatic tissue, is the surgical gold standard, although other technologies such as enucleation and open removal exist.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Sildenafil does not relieve outlet obstruction and combined with his alpha-1 blocker may cause significant hypotension.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Watchful waiting is inappropriate once complications such as rising creatinine, stones, and recurrent UTIs have appeared.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A prolonged fluoroquinolone course treats chronic bacterial prostatitis; his UTIs stem from obstruction that must be relieved.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Switching between alpha-1A-selective agents does not address failure of maximal medical therapy with established complications.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man has mild urinary frequency. His PSA is 12.4 ng/mL, and digital rectal examination shows an enlarged gland with an area of questionable irregularity. He is afebrile, urinalysis is normal, and serum creatinine is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Prostate biopsy

choices.label: B
choices.text: Finasteride with repeat PSA in 1 year

choices.label: C
choices.text: Transurethral resection of the prostate

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pre- and post-prostatic massage urine cultures

choices.label: E
choices.text: Empiric ciprofloxacin for 4 to 6 weeks

explanation.summary: Biopsy differentiates prostate cancer from benign tissue when PSA is elevated and DRE findings are normal or questionable.
explanation.whyCorrect: PSA in BPH is often only mildly elevated and commonly stays below 10 ng/mL, and irregularity or asymmetry on DRE raises concern for cancer nodules. Biopsy is the test that differentiates prostate cancer from benign prostate tissue in the setting of an elevated PSA with normal or questionable DRE findings.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Treating presumptively for BPH and waiting a year would delay diagnosis of a possible malignancy suggested by this PSA and exam.
whyWrongByChoice.C: TURP is a treatment for obstructive symptoms refractory to medical therapy, not a way to evaluate a suspicious PSA and exam.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pre- and post-massage cultures are used to diagnose chronic bacterial prostatitis; he has no recurrent UTIs or pelvic pain.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Prolonged antibiotics treat chronic bacterial prostatitis, and his normal urinalysis and absence of pain argue against infection.

questions.stem: Among men who present with symptomatic prostatitis, which of the following types accounts for the large majority of cases?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acute bacterial prostatitis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chronic bacterial prostatitis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Chronic pelvic pain syndrome (CP/CPPS)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Asymptomatic inflammatory prostatitis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Granulomatous prostatitis

explanation.summary: CP/CPPS is the most common type of prostatitis, responsible for roughly 90% of symptomatic cases.
explanation.whyCorrect: Of the four NIH types, chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome is by far the most common, accounting for around 90% of symptomatic prostatitis. It presents with unexplained chronic pain in the groin, genitals, or perineum for more than 3 months with a normal urinalysis and negative cultures.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acute bacterial prostatitis is explicitly uncommon, presenting as a severe febrile UTI with an exquisitely tender gland.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chronic bacterial prostatitis occurs in middle-aged men with recurrent mild UTIs but is far less common than CP/CPPS.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Type 4 prostatitis is by definition asymptomatic and found incidentally, so it does not account for symptomatic presentations.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Granulomatous prostatitis is an uncommon tissue reaction to infection or to stimuli such as intravesical BCG.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old man admitted with acute bacterial prostatitis has a temperature of 39.2 C and an exquisitely tender prostate. Twelve hours after admission he has been unable to pass urine, has suprapubic pain, and has a bladder palpable midway to the umbilicus. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Suprapubic catheter placement

choices.label: B
choices.text: Transurethral catheter placement

choices.label: C
choices.text: Prostatic massage to relieve the obstruction

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ultrasound-guided drainage of the prostate

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transurethral resection of the prostate

explanation.summary: Urinary retention complicating acute prostatitis is relieved with a suprapubic catheter that bypasses the inflamed gland.
explanation.whyCorrect: Potential complications of acute prostatitis include urinary retention and prostatic abscess. Urinary retention may require drainage by suprapubic catheter, which bypasses the inflamed prostate rather than forcing an instrument through it.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Passing a catheter through the acutely inflamed prostatic urethra is what the suprapubic route is specifically chosen to avoid.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Massage is a diagnostic maneuver for chronic prostatitis; vigorous manipulation of an acutely inflamed gland is avoided.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ultrasound-guided drainage treats a prostatic abscess, a collection of pus and bacteria, which has not been demonstrated here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TURP is the surgical treatment for BPH refractory to medical therapy, not a maneuver for acute infectious retention.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with acute bacterial prostatitis has taken ciprofloxacin for 5 days but continues to have fevers to 39 C and worsening perineal pain. Blood pressure is stable. Transrectal ultrasonography demonstrates a 3-cm fluid collection within the prostate. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ultrasound-guided drainage of the collection

choices.label: B
choices.text: Continuation of the same antibiotic for 6 weeks

choices.label: C
choices.text: Placement of a suprapubic catheter

choices.label: D
choices.text: Warm baths with an NSAID and tamsulosin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transurethral resection of the prostate

explanation.summary: A prostatic abscess complicating acute prostatitis is treated with surgical or ultrasound-guided drainage.
explanation.whyCorrect: A prostatic abscess is a collection of pus and bacteria in the prostate and is a recognized complication of acute bacterial prostatitis. It is treated with surgical or ultrasound-guided drainage; antibiotics alone do not clear an established collection, which is why his fevers persist.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Extended fluoroquinolone courses are the treatment of chronic bacterial prostatitis; here a drainable collection is the reason for treatment failure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A suprapubic catheter is used for urinary retention complicating acute prostatitis, and he is voiding without retention.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Warm baths, NSAIDs, and alpha-1 blockers are supportive therapy for CP/CPPS, which has no bacterial cause and no abscess.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TURP removes hyperplastic tissue in refractory BPH and is not the described treatment for a prostatic abscess.

questions.stem: A 37-year-old man comes to the emergency department with fever, chills, burning on urination, and severe rectal pain, and acute bacterial prostatitis is suspected. Which of the following is the most appropriate approach to examining his prostate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Gentle examination, avoiding vigorous palpation of the gland

choices.label: B
choices.text: Vigorous massage with culture of the expressed fluid

choices.label: C
choices.text: Deferral of any rectal examination until cultures return

choices.label: D
choices.text: Repeated massage every 48 hours during antibiotic therapy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Examination only after 6 weeks of antibiotic treatment

explanation.summary: In acute prostatitis the gland is examined gently; vigorous digital rectal examination is avoided.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acute prostatitis is associated with very severe perirectal pain and perineal tenderness, and a vigorous digital rectal examination should be avoided because it can be extremely painful and may theoretically increase the risk of bacteremia. A gentle examination still reveals the enlarged, tender gland that supports the diagnosis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Prostatic massage is the diagnostic maneuver for chronic prostatitis and is precisely the vigorous manipulation to avoid acutely.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The examination is not deferred; it is performed gently, and urinalysis and urine culture are obtained alongside it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Serial massage has no role in acute prostatitis, which is diagnosed clinically with urinalysis and culture and treated with antibiotics.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Waiting weeks to examine the patient would delay recognition of the enlarged, inflamed gland and its complications.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old sexually active man develops fever, dysuria, and perineal pain 1 week after an episode of urethral discharge. He has never had a urinary catheter placed or a prostate biopsy. Which of the following best describes how bacteria most likely reached his prostate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Retrograde spread from the urethra into the prostatic ducts

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hematogenous seeding from a distant skin infection

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lymphatic spread from an inflamed rectosigmoid colon

choices.label: D
choices.text: Direct extension from an infected seminal vesicle stone

choices.label: E
choices.text: Inoculation of the gland during urinary instrumentation

explanation.summary: Acute prostatitis usually follows retrograde spread of urethral organisms, including reflux of infected urine into prostatic ducts.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acute prostatitis may occur as part of a sexually transmitted infection or from retrograde spread of bacteria from the urethra into the prostate, including reflux of infected urine into the prostatic ducts. His preceding urethral discharge and absence of instrumentation fit this ascending route.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Bloodstream seeding from a remote site is not among the described routes by which organisms reach the prostate.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lymphatic spread from bowel inflammation is not a described mechanism; bowel disease is something to exclude, not a source.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Direct extension from a seminal vesicle stone is not a recognized route of prostatic infection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Catheterization and prostate biopsy are recognized precipitants, but he has had neither procedure.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man has had three episodes of mild urinary tract infection over 8 months, accompanied by low back pain and perineal discomfort but no fever or chills. Which of the following elements of his history would most increase his risk for chronic bacterial prostatitis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A prior episode of epididymitis

choices.label: B
choices.text: A vasectomy performed 10 years ago

choices.label: C
choices.text: Daily NSAID use for knee osteoarthritis

choices.label: D
choices.text: A father diagnosed with prostate cancer

choices.label: E
choices.text: A 20-pack-year history of cigarette smoking

explanation.summary: Other genitourinary infections, catheter placement, and anal intercourse are the risk factors for chronic bacterial prostatitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chronic bacterial prostatitis results from chronic colonization of the gland by bacteria, most often E. coli. Recognized risk factors are other genitourinary infections such as cystitis and epididymitis, urinary catheter placement, and anal intercourse, so his prior epididymitis is the relevant exposure.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Vasectomy is not listed among the exposures that predispose to chronic colonization of the prostate.
whyWrongByChoice.C: NSAIDs are used as supportive therapy in CP/CPPS; they are not a risk factor for bacterial colonization of the gland.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Family history bears on prostate cancer risk and PSA interpretation, not on chronic bacterial infection of the prostate.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Smoking is not among the described risk factors for chronic bacterial prostatitis.

questions.stem: Microscopic examination of prostatic tissue from a man with an acutely symptomatic prostate shows an intensely inflamed gland with sheets of neutrophils. Which of the following clinical presentations is most consistent with this histologic finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fever, chills, urinary burning, and severe rectal pain

choices.label: B
choices.text: Recurrent mild urinary infections over 6 months without fever

choices.label: C
choices.text: Four months of perineal pain with negative urine cultures

choices.label: D
choices.text: Incidental white blood cells on urinalysis without symptoms

choices.label: E
choices.text: Gradual weak stream and nocturia with a smooth gland

explanation.summary: Neutrophils in an intensely inflamed prostate are the histologic signature of acute bacterial prostatitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: In acute bacterial prostatitis the gland is intensely inflamed and neutrophils are seen on histologic examination. Clinically this corresponds to a severe UTI picture with fever, chills, urinary burning, frequency, and rectal pain, often with difficulty voiding from the swollen gland.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Recurrent mild UTIs without systemic symptoms describe chronic bacterial prostatitis, whose infiltrate is lymphocytes and plasma cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Months of perineal pain with negative cultures indicate CP/CPPS, which lacks a bacterial cause and this acute neutrophilic reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Incidental WBCs without symptoms define asymptomatic inflammatory prostatitis, not an acutely inflamed neutrophil-rich gland.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A slowly weakening stream with a smooth enlarged prostate is BPH, which shows glandular hyperplasia rather than acute inflammation.

questions.stem: A 49-year-old man with recurrent mild urinary tract infections and perineal discomfort is diagnosed with chronic bacterial prostatitis and treated with ciprofloxacin for 7 days. His symptoms improve, then recur 3 weeks later with the same organism on culture. Which of the following is the most appropriate management now?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ciprofloxacin continued for 4 to 6 weeks

choices.label: B
choices.text: A second 7-day course of ciprofloxacin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Tamsulosin with warm baths and NSAIDs

choices.label: D
choices.text: Suprapubic catheter drainage of the bladder

choices.label: E
choices.text: No further therapy, as the process is self-limited

explanation.summary: Chronic bacterial prostatitis is an indwelling infection requiring 4-6 weeks of antibiotics, not a short course.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chronic bacterial prostatitis reflects chronic colonization of the gland, and these indwelling infections require longer antibiotic courses for eradication than acute prostatitis. A fluoroquinolone is the preferred empiric agent, continued for 4 to 6 weeks, with a second course given as needed.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Repeating a short course reproduces the inadequate duration that allowed the organism to persist in the gland.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Alpha-1 blockers, warm baths, and NSAIDs are the supportive regimen for CP/CPPS, which has no cultured organism.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Suprapubic drainage addresses urinary retention complicating acute prostatitis, and he is not in retention.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Asymptomatic inflammatory prostatitis is the self-limited type needing no therapy; this is a documented bacterial infection.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man with chronic bacterial prostatitis develops a severe diffuse rash after two doses of ciprofloxacin, and the drug is stopped. His urine culture grew Escherichia coli susceptible to multiple agents. Which of the following is the most appropriate alternative therapy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole

choices.label: B
choices.text: Tamsulosin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Finasteride

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sildenafil

choices.label: E
choices.text: Warm baths with an NSAID alone

explanation.summary: When a fluoroquinolone cannot be used for chronic bacterial prostatitis, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole or azithromycin is the alternative.
explanation.whyCorrect: Empiric treatment of chronic bacterial prostatitis is best with a fluoroquinolone, with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole or azithromycin as alternative options. Whichever agent is used, it is continued for 4 to 6 weeks, with a second course as needed.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Alpha-1 blockers relax prostatic smooth muscle and may help CP/CPPS symptoms, but they do not eradicate a bacterial infection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors reduce prostatic hyperplasia in BPH and have no antimicrobial activity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sildenafil is a PDE-5 inhibitor for erectile dysfunction with no role in treating prostatic infection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Supportive measures alone are appropriate for CP/CPPS; a cultured bacterial infection requires antibiotic therapy.

questions.stem: A 43-year-old man has had 5 months of perineal and genital pain with intermittent irritative voiding symptoms. Urinalysis is normal, prostatic fluid after massage shows no bacteria, and cultures are negative. He asks what caused his condition. Which of the following is the most accurate statement about its cause?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The cause is unknown and may involve trauma or autoimmunity

choices.label: B
choices.text: It follows chronic colonization of the gland by Escherichia coli

choices.label: C
choices.text: It results from dihydrotestosterone-driven glandular hyperplasia

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a tissue reaction to bacillus Calmette-Guerin exposure

choices.label: E
choices.text: It arises from reflux of infected urine into prostatic ducts

explanation.summary: In CP/CPPS the exact cause is unknown; trauma, autoimmune attack, or reaction to normal prostate flora are proposed.
explanation.whyCorrect: His chronic pelvic pain beyond 3 months with a normal urinalysis and negative cultures identifies CP/CPPS. It is characterized by chronic pelvic pain without evidence of bacterial infection, and although the exact cause is unknown, the inflammation may be secondary to trauma, an autoimmune attack, or a reaction to normal prostate flora.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Chronic colonization by E. coli defines chronic bacterial prostatitis, which shows bacteria on post-massage culture; his cultures are negative.
whyWrongByChoice.C: DHT-driven hyperplasia produces BPH with obstructive voiding symptoms, not months of perineal and genital pain.
whyWrongByChoice.D: BCG exposure produces granulomatous prostatitis, diagnosed histologically by granulomas, and he has had no such treatment.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reflux of infected urine into prostatic ducts is a route to acute bacterial prostatitis, a febrile illness with an infected urinalysis.

questions.stem: A 51-year-old man with recurrent mild urinary tract infections and a boggy prostate is evaluated for chronic bacterial prostatitis. Urine is collected before prostatic massage, and the massage is continued until a milky urethral discharge appears, which is cultured with the post-massage urine. Which of the following findings would best support the diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A tenfold increase in bacteria in the post-massage specimen

choices.label: B
choices.text: White blood cells in the post-massage specimen with sterile cultures

choices.label: C
choices.text: Equal numbers of bacteria in the pre- and post-massage specimens

choices.label: D
choices.text: A PSA value that falls below 4 ng/mL after the massage

choices.label: E
choices.text: Absence of bacteria in both specimens with negative cultures

explanation.summary: Chronic bacterial prostatitis is supported when post-massage bacteria are tenfold higher than in the pre-massage urine.
explanation.whyCorrect: Urine is sampled before and after prostatic massage, which is performed for up to a minute or until a milky discharge emerges, and the discharge is cultured along with the urine. If bacteria are seen, the post-massage specimen should show a tenfold increase in bacteria compared with the pre-massage urine, localizing the infection to the prostate. Note that bacteria are cultured in only about 10% of patients, so a negative study does not exclude the diagnosis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: White blood cells without organisms are the pattern of CP/CPPS or asymptomatic inflammatory prostatitis, not of bacterial localization.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Equal counts fail to localize infection to the prostate, since the post-massage rise is what implicates the gland.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PSA is elevated in all forms of prostatitis and is measured to exclude cancer; it is not tracked across the massage.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Negative studies are the expected picture in CP/CPPS, a diagnosis of exclusion, rather than support for bacterial prostatitis.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man undergoes a routine health maintenance examination. Digital rectal examination reveals a firm, irregular nodule on the posterior surface of the prostate, and subsequent biopsy demonstrates adenocarcinoma. In which of the following regions of the prostate did this tumor most likely arise?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Central zone

choices.label: B
choices.text: Transitional zone

choices.label: C
choices.text: Peripheral zone

choices.label: D
choices.text: Prostatic urethra

choices.label: E
choices.text: Seminal vesicles

explanation.summary: Prostate adenocarcinoma typically arises in the peripheral zone, which corresponds to the posterior lobe palpable on rectal exam.
