explanation.whyCorrect: The three Ps of prostate cancer are Primary, Posterior lobe, and Peripheral zone. Because the peripheral zone lies along the outer, posterior edge of the gland, tumors there are readily felt as irregular nodularity on digital rectal examination.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The central zone is a periurethral region classically involved in benign prostatic hyperplasia, not the usual site of adenocarcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The transitional zone is the other periurethral zone typical of benign prostatic hyperplasia, which compresses the urethra rather than presenting as a posterior nodule.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The prostatic urethra is compressed by periurethral hyperplasia; it is not the tissue of origin for prostatic adenocarcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The seminal vesicles are removed with the prostate at radical prostatectomy but are not where primary prostate cancer arises.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man is diagnosed with localized prostate adenocarcinoma after an elevated screening PSA. He is surprised because he has no urinary symptoms, while his brother with benign prostatic hyperplasia has severe hesitancy and a weak stream. Which of the following best explains why this patient's cancer has remained asymptomatic?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The tumor arose in the periurethral transitional zone

choices.label: B
choices.text: The tumor arose in the peripheral zone, away from the urethra

choices.label: C
choices.text: The tumor shrinks the gland rather than enlarging it

choices.label: D
choices.text: The tumor suppresses androgen signaling in the bladder neck

choices.label: E
choices.text: The tumor secretes PSA, which relaxes the prostatic urethra

explanation.summary: Prostate cancer is usually asymptomatic because it begins in the peripheral zone, distant from the prostatic urethra.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because prostate cancer typically starts along the outer edges of the gland in the peripheral zone, it does not compress the urethra early in its course. In contrast, benign prostatic hyperplasia involves the periurethral central and transitional zones, so it produces obstructive urinary symptoms much earlier.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The transitional zone is the classic location of benign prostatic hyperplasia; a periurethral tumor would tend to cause urinary symptoms, not silence.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Prostate cancer forms a solid tumor within the gland; it does not shrink the prostate, and gland size is not why early cancer is silent.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Prostate cancer cells depend on androgen signaling for growth; the tumor does not suppress androgen effects elsewhere.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PSA is a protein secreted by prostatic epithelial cells used for detection; it has no urethra-relaxing action.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old man asks about his chance of developing prostate cancer. His father was diagnosed with prostate adenocarcinoma at age 58. He drinks two beers most weekends, works as an accountant, and had a urinary tract infection in his 20s. Which of the following features of his history most increases his risk of prostate cancer?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A first-degree relative diagnosed before age 65

choices.label: B
choices.text: A remote history of urinary tract infection

choices.label: C
choices.text: Regular weekend alcohol consumption

choices.label: D
choices.text: A sedentary desk occupation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Being younger than 60 years of age

explanation.summary: A first-degree relative diagnosed with prostate cancer before age 65 raises a man's risk severalfold.
explanation.whyCorrect: Prostate cancer has a strong familial component, and having a first-degree relative diagnosed before age 65 increases risk severalfold. Other established risk factors include increasing age (incidence rises after 50), African American race, and genetic abnormalities such as BRCA2 and MYC.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A remote urinary tract infection is not a described risk factor for prostate cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Alcohol use is not among the risk factors described; dietary fat and red meat intake are only probable associations with inconsistent evidence.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Occupation and sedentary work are not described risk factors for prostate carcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Younger age is protective, not a risk; incidence increases in men older than 50 years.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man undergoes transrectal ultrasound-guided core biopsy for an elevated PSA and an irregular prostatic nodule. Microscopy shows small, crowded glands lying back-to-back between larger benign glands, lined by a single layer of cuboidal cells with enlarged nuclei and prominent nucleoli. Which of the following additional findings would confirm that these glands are malignant?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Loss of the outer basal cell layer

choices.label: B
choices.text: Preservation of a two-layered glandular epithelium

choices.label: C
choices.text: Abundant fibromuscular stroma between the glands

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tall columnar cells with small, inconspicuous nucleoli

choices.label: E
choices.text: Widely spaced tubuloalveolar glands of uniform size

explanation.summary: Loss of the basal cell layer characterizes prostate adenocarcinoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: Normal prostatic glands have a two-layered epithelium: an inner columnar secretory layer and an outer flattened regenerative (basal) layer. Adenocarcinoma arises from the secretory layer, so the basal layer is lost and malignant glands are lined by a single layer of cuboidal cells with enlarged nuclei and visible nucleoli.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A two-layered epithelium is the architecture of benign prostatic glands; its preservation argues against carcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Malignant glands are characteristically back-to-back with no intervening stroma; abundant stroma between glands is a feature of normal tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Malignant cells show enlarged nuclei with prominent nucleoli; small inconspicuous nucleoli suggest benign epithelium.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Widely spaced tubuloalveolar glands in fibromuscular stroma describe normal prostate, not the small crowded glands of adenocarcinoma.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with a PSA of 4.6 ng/mL undergoes transrectal ultrasound-guided core biopsy of the prostate; all 12 cores show benign tissue. One week later, before any new symptoms develop, a repeat PSA drawn in error returns at 8.9 ng/mL. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for the higher value?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Interval development of prostatic adenocarcinoma

choices.label: B
choices.text: Recent instrumentation and manipulation of the prostate

choices.label: C
choices.text: Age-related enlargement of the gland over the interval

choices.label: D
choices.text: New osteoblastic metastases releasing antigen

choices.label: E
choices.text: Loss of PSA secretion by benign epithelial cells

explanation.summary: PSA is not specific for cancer; procedures that manipulate the prostate, such as biopsy, elevate it.
explanation.whyCorrect: PSA is secreted by prostatic epithelial cells and rises with prostatitis, benign prostatic hyperplasia, urinary retention, and procedures that manipulate the prostate such as biopsy. A PSA drawn one week after a 12-core biopsy is expected to be falsely elevated by the procedure itself.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A cancer large enough to double the PSA would not develop in one week, and 12 cores were just benign.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Prostate size does increase PSA with age, but that occurs over years, not one week.
whyWrongByChoice.D: There is no evidence of malignancy, and bony metastases occur in advanced cancer, not after a benign biopsy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Benign epithelial cells continue to secrete PSA; losing secretion would lower the level, not raise it.

questions.stem: A healthy, asymptomatic 74-year-old man requests prostate cancer screening after shared decision-making. His PSA returns at 5.9 ng/mL, and digital rectal examination is unremarkable. Using age-specific PSA reference ranges, which of the following is the most accurate interpretation of this result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It falls within the reference range for his age group

choices.label: B
choices.text: It exceeds the reference range for any age group

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is diagnostic of prostatic adenocarcinoma

choices.label: D
choices.text: It indicates urinary retention requiring catheterization

choices.label: E
choices.text: It can only be interpreted after a bone scan

explanation.summary: Age-specific PSA reference ranges rise with age; for men 70-79 years the range is 0-6.5 ng/mL.
explanation.whyCorrect: PSA increases with age even in healthy men because the prostate enlarges. The age-specific reference range for 70-79 years is 0-6.5 ng/mL, so a value of 5.9 ng/mL is within range for this 74-year-old, whereas the same value would exceed the 0-4.5 ng/mL range for a man in his 60s.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The 70-79 year reference range extends to 6.5 ng/mL, so 5.9 ng/mL does not exceed it.
whyWrongByChoice.C: No PSA level is diagnostic of cancer; biopsy is the only way to truly diagnose prostate cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Urinary retention can elevate PSA, but this asymptomatic man has no evidence of retention, and the value itself does not indicate it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Bone scans are used in staging patients with worrisome established cancer, not for interpreting a screening PSA.

questions.stem: A prostate biopsy report describes the two most prevalent architectural patterns of a tumor: the predominant pattern shows well-formed glands with some cells invading surrounding tissue, and the secondary pattern shows few glands with invading cells. The pathologist assigns these patterns grades of 3 and 4, respectively. Which of the following is this tumor's Gleason score?

explanation.summary: The Gleason score sums the two most prevalent architectural patterns, yielding a score of 2-10.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gleason grading evaluates the tumor's architectural pattern, picking the two most prevalent patterns from the biopsy and combining them into a score of 2-10. Patterns of 3 and 4 sum to a Gleason score of 7. Higher scores predict more aggressive disease and poorer outcomes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 3 is only the predominant single pattern; the score requires adding the second most prevalent pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 4 is only the secondary pattern grade, not the combined score.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 10 is the maximum possible score, reached only when both patterns are grade 5 sheets of cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 12 is outside the Gleason system, which ranges from 2 to 10.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old man presents with 2 months of progressive low back pain. Radiographs show multiple dense, sclerotic lesions within the lumbar vertebral bodies and pelvis. Which of the following primary malignancies is the most likely source of these lesions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Prostatic adenocarcinoma

choices.label: B
choices.text: Renal cell carcinoma

choices.label: C
choices.text: Multiple myeloma

choices.label: D
choices.text: Urothelial carcinoma of the bladder

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hepatocellular carcinoma

explanation.summary: Osteoblastic bony metastases in a male point strongly to a prostate primary.
explanation.whyCorrect: Prostate cancer spreads hematogenously, especially to the spine, and its bony metastases are typically osteoblastic, appearing as dense sclerotic lesions. The bones most commonly involved are the lumbar spine, proximal femur, pelvis, thoracic spine, and ribs, matching this man's imaging.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Renal cell carcinoma does not characteristically produce the osteoblastic pattern that points to a prostate origin in males.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Multiple myeloma produces destructive marrow lesions rather than the dense sclerotic lesions typical of prostate metastases.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Urothelial carcinoma is not the classic source of diffusely sclerotic vertebral and pelvic lesions in an elderly man.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hepatocellular carcinoma is not the malignancy classically linked to osteoblastic spine metastases in males.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man in excellent health is found to have low-risk prostatic adenocarcinoma on biopsy. His life expectancy exceeds 20 years. He is a good candidate for curative treatment but wishes to safely defer it as long as possible to avoid erectile dysfunction and incontinence. Which of the following management plans is most appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Watchful waiting with palliative treatment if symptoms develop

choices.label: B
choices.text: Active surveillance with serial PSA, rectal exams, and biopsies

choices.label: C
choices.text: Androgen deprivation therapy alone for the localized tumor

choices.label: D
choices.text: Docetaxel chemotherapy to eradicate the localized disease

choices.label: E
choices.text: Bilateral orchiectomy to achieve castrate testosterone levels

explanation.summary: Active surveillance suits low-risk patients with good life expectancy who wish to defer curative treatment while remaining candidates for it.
explanation.whyCorrect: Active surveillance is indicated for patients with good life expectancy (over 10-20 years) and low-risk disease who are good candidates for curative treatment but want to defer it to avoid adverse effects. It involves active monitoring with regular PSA tests, digital rectal examinations, and prostate biopsies, with curative treatment still available if the disease progresses.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Watchful waiting abandons curative intent and is reserved for patients with limited life expectancy under 10 years, not a healthy man with more than 20 years.
whyWrongByChoice.C: ADT alone is not routine treatment for low-risk localized disease; it backbones therapy for recurrent or metastatic cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Docetaxel is systemic treatment for advanced or metastatic prostate cancer, not a curative option for low-risk localized disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Orchiectomy is a permanent form of androgen deprivation used in advanced disease and would impose the very adverse effects he wants to avoid.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer and painful vertebral metastases is scheduled to begin leuprolide. His oncologist is concerned that starting this drug could transiently worsen his bone pain and even precipitate spinal cord compression. Which of the following medications should be given when initiating therapy to limit this complication?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Flutamide

choices.label: B
choices.text: Prednisone

choices.label: C
choices.text: Goserelin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Docetaxel

choices.label: E
choices.text: Abiraterone

explanation.summary: A first-generation androgen-receptor antagonist such as flutamide is used when starting a GnRH agonist to limit the testosterone flare.
explanation.whyCorrect: GnRH agonists such as leuprolide initially stimulate pituitary GnRH receptors, transiently increasing LH and testosterone before receptor desensitization lowers them. This flare can worsen bone pain, urinary obstruction, or spinal cord compression, so a short course of an androgen-receptor antagonist, classically the first-generation agent flutamide, is given to block the flare's effects on the tumor.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A glucocorticoid is co-administered with abiraterone to offset mineralocorticoid excess, not with leuprolide for flare protection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Goserelin is another GnRH agonist and would produce the same initial testosterone flare, not prevent it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Docetaxel is a microtubule-stabilizing chemotherapy for advanced disease; it does not block androgen-receptor activation during a flare.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Abiraterone lowers androgen synthesis via CYP17 inhibition but is not the described short-course agent for covering a GnRH agonist flare.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer begins a new oral agent that decreases androgen synthesis in the testes, adrenal glands, and tumor tissue. Six weeks later he has a blood pressure of 168/96 mm Hg, serum potassium of 2.9 mEq/L, and new lower-extremity edema. Which of the following best explains these findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CYP17 inhibition shifting steroid synthesis toward mineralocorticoid excess

choices.label: B
choices.text: Androgen-receptor blockade causing renal sodium and water wasting

choices.label: C
choices.text: GnRH-receptor desensitization stimulating adrenal catecholamine release

choices.label: D
choices.text: Microtubule stabilization impairing cardiac and vascular contractility

choices.label: E
choices.text: Direct activation of glucocorticoid receptors by the drug itself

explanation.summary: Abiraterone inhibits CYP17, and the resulting fall in cortisol promotes mineralocorticoid excess with hypertension, hypokalemia, and edema.
explanation.whyCorrect: The drug described is abiraterone, a CYP17 inhibitor that decreases androgen synthesis in the testes, adrenals, and tumor. Because CYP17 inhibition also decreases cortisol and promotes mineralocorticoid excess, patients develop hypertension, hypokalemia, and edema, which is why abiraterone is administered with a glucocorticoid.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Androgen-receptor antagonists cause hepatotoxicity, gynecomastia, and sexual dysfunction, not a mineralocorticoid-excess picture, and sodium wasting would lower blood pressure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: GnRH-receptor desensitization is the mechanism of GnRH agonists and does not produce catecholamine-driven hypokalemia and edema.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Microtubule stabilization is the mechanism of docetaxel and does not explain hypertension with hypokalemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Abiraterone reduces cortisol rather than acting as a glucocorticoid agonist; a glucocorticoid must be added alongside it.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with castration-resistant metastatic prostate cancer is started on docetaxel. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of this drug?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Stabilizes microtubules and prevents mitosis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Inhibits CYP17-mediated androgen synthesis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Blocks pituitary GnRH receptors directly

choices.label: D
choices.text: Antagonizes androgen receptors in tumor cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Desensitizes GnRH receptors with continuous stimulation

explanation.summary: Docetaxel is a taxane microtubule inhibitor that stabilizes microtubules and prevents mitosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Docetaxel is a taxane that stabilizes microtubules, preventing mitosis in dividing tumor cells. It is used as part of systemic treatment for advanced or metastatic prostate cancer, including selected castration-sensitive disease and castration-resistant disease.

whyWrongByChoice.B: CYP17 inhibition is the mechanism of abiraterone, which decreases androgen synthesis in the testes, adrenals, and tumor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Direct blockade of pituitary GnRH receptors describes GnRH antagonists such as degarelix and relugolix.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Androgen-receptor antagonism describes bicalutamide, flutamide, and enzalutamide.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Receptor desensitization from continuous stimulation is the mechanism of GnRH agonists such as leuprolide and goserelin.

questions.stem: A 56-year-old man says he has heard that prostate cancer is extremely common but rarely fatal, and he wants to know the actual numbers before deciding about screening. Which of the following best describes the lifetime probability of diagnosis and of death from prostate cancer among males in the United States?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 3% are diagnosed in their lifetime and about 1% die of it

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 50% are diagnosed in their lifetime and about 20% die of it

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 20% are diagnosed in their lifetime and about 3% die of it

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 20% are diagnosed in their lifetime and about 15% die of it

choices.label: E
choices.text: About 10% are diagnosed in their lifetime and about 10% die of it

explanation.summary: About 20% of U.S. males develop prostate cancer, but only about 3% die of it.
explanation.whyCorrect: Prostate cancer is the most common non-skin cancer in U.S. males and most commonly affects men over age 50. Roughly 20% of males develop the disease during their lifetime, yet only about 3% die from it, reflecting its usually slow, asymptomatic course. It nonetheless remains the second-leading cause of cancer death in males after lung cancer, and the fifth leading cause of cancer death overall.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This understates incidence; about 20%, not 3%, of males are diagnosed during their lifetime.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Neither figure is correct; lifetime diagnosis is about 20% and mortality about 3%.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mortality is far lower than incidence; only about 3% of males die of prostate cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Incidence is about twice this figure and mortality is far lower, since most men die of unrelated causes.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old African American man with no family history of malignancy asks how his background affects his chance of developing prostate cancer compared with other men his age. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: His risk is lower than that of Asian American men

choices.label: B
choices.text: Race has no measurable effect on prostate cancer incidence

choices.label: C
choices.text: His risk is higher than that of White and Asian American men

choices.label: D
choices.text: His risk becomes elevated only after he reaches age 70

choices.label: E
choices.text: His risk is the same as that of Asian American men

explanation.summary: Prostate cancer incidence is higher in African American males and lower in Asian American males.
explanation.whyCorrect: Prostate cancer rates differ markedly across populations. The disease is more common in African Americans and less common in Asian Americans, making race/ethnicity an established risk factor alongside age, family history, and genetic abnormalities such as BRCA2 and MYC.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The gradient runs the other way: risk is higher in African Americans and lower in Asian Americans.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Rates differ markedly across populations, so race/ethnicity is a recognized risk factor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Incidence begins to rise in males older than 50 years, not only after age 70.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Asian Americans have a lower incidence, so the two groups are not equivalent.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old man with a strong family cancer history undergoes germline genetic testing. Identification of which of the following abnormalities would most increase his risk of prostate adenocarcinoma?

choices.label: A
choices.text: RET proto-oncogene mutation

choices.label: B
choices.text: BRCA2 mutation

choices.label: C
choices.text: APC mutation

choices.label: D
choices.text: VHL mutation

choices.label: E
choices.text: RB1 mutation

explanation.summary: BRCA2 is among the genetic abnormalities associated with prostate cancer.
explanation.whyCorrect: Prostate cancer has a strong familial component, and specific genetic abnormalities have been associated with it, notably BRCA2 and MYC. A first-degree relative diagnosed before age 65 also raises risk severalfold.

whyWrongByChoice.A: RET is not among the abnormalities described in association with prostate adenocarcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: APC is not one of the genetic abnormalities linked to prostate cancer risk.
whyWrongByChoice.D: VHL is not described as conferring increased prostate cancer risk.
whyWrongByChoice.E: RB1 is not among the genetic abnormalities associated with prostate adenocarcinoma.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with metastatic prostate adenocarcinoma begins therapy that lowers his serum testosterone to castrate levels, and his disease regresses. Which of the following best explains why lowering testosterone controls his tumor?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Testosterone is required for renal clearance of PSA

choices.label: B
choices.text: Androgens suppress immune recognition of tumor cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Testosterone stimulates osteoblastic activity in bone metastases

choices.label: D
choices.text: Androgens are converted to carcinogens within prostate tissue

choices.label: E
choices.text: Prostate cancer cells depend on androgens for growth and survival

explanation.summary: Most prostate cancers depend on androgen-receptor signaling, which is why androgen deprivation controls the disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Prostate cancer cells rely on androgens for their growth and survival, and most prostate cancers initially depend on androgen-receptor signaling. Androgen deprivation therapy exploits this by lowering testicular testosterone to castrate levels, either permanently by bilateral orchiectomy or pharmacologically by medical castration.

whyWrongByChoice.A: PSA is a protein secreted by prostatic epithelial cells; its clearance is not the reason androgen deprivation works.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Androgen deprivation works by withdrawing a growth requirement of the tumor cells, not by restoring immune recognition.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Osteoblastic bone lesions are a feature of prostate metastases, but androgen withdrawal treats the tumor itself rather than bone turnover.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Androgens act as growth and survival signals through the androgen receptor; conversion to carcinogens is not the described mechanism.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man reports 2 years of urinary hesitancy, a weak stream, and postvoid dribbling. Digital rectal examination shows a smoothly enlarged, non-nodular prostate, and his PSA is within the reference range for his age. Enlargement of which of the following regions best explains his symptoms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The peripheral zone along the posterior lobe

choices.label: B
choices.text: The periurethral central and transitional zones

choices.label: C
choices.text: The seminal vesicles and ejaculatory ducts

choices.label: D
choices.text: The membranous urethra and external sphincter

choices.label: E
choices.text: The bladder trigone and ureteric orifices

explanation.summary: Benign prostatic hyperplasia involves the periurethral central and transitional zones, compressing the prostatic urethra.
explanation.whyCorrect: Benign prostatic hyperplasia typically involves the periurethral central and transitional zones, classically associated with the median and adjacent lateral lobes. Growth in these zones compresses the prostatic urethra and produces obstructive urinary symptoms, in contrast to prostate cancer, which arises peripherally and is usually silent.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The peripheral zone corresponds to the posterior lobe and is the site of prostate cancer; lesions there lie away from the urethra and rarely obstruct early.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The seminal vesicles are not the site of the hyperplasia that narrows the prostatic urethra.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The membranous urethra and external sphincter lie distal to the prostate and are not the enlarged tissue in this presentation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The trigone and ureteric orifices are bladder structures, not prostatic zones that enlarge in hyperplasia.

questions.stem: A radical prostatectomy specimen from a 64-year-old man shows small malignant glands tracking circumferentially around nerve bundles within and at the edge of the gland. Which of the following best describes the significance of this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lymphatic spread to the internal iliac lymph nodes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hematogenous spread producing osteoblastic lesions

choices.label: C
choices.text: Perineural invasion contributing to local tumor extension

choices.label: D
choices.text: A benign finding common in normal prostatic tissue

choices.label: E
choices.text: Direct extension from the transitional zone into the urethra

explanation.summary: Perineural invasion is a characteristic pathologic feature of prostate cancer that may contribute to local tumor extension.
explanation.whyCorrect: Prostate cancer spreads by local extension, lymphatic dissemination, and hematogenous routes. Perineural invasion, in which malignant glands surround and track along nerves, is a characteristic pathologic feature of prostate adenocarcinoma and may contribute to extension of the tumor beyond the gland.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lymphatic dissemination involves regional pelvic nodes and would be demonstrated in node specimens, not by tumor encircling intraprostatic nerves.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hematogenous spread produces distant osteoblastic bone lesions rather than this intraglandular pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tumor cells tracking along nerves is a malignant feature, not a finding of normal prostatic tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Prostate adenocarcinoma arises in the peripheral zone; this pattern describes nerve-associated invasion, not periurethral extension.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with newly diagnosed prostate adenocarcinoma undergoes imaging that shows enlarged regional lymph nodes. Which of the following nodal groups is most likely involved by lymphatic dissemination of this tumor?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Superficial inguinal lymph nodes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Para-aortic lymph nodes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Left supraclavicular lymph nodes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Internal iliac lymph nodes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mediastinal lymph nodes

explanation.summary: Prostate cancer disseminates lymphatically to regional pelvic nodes, usually the internal iliac nodes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Prostate cancer commonly spreads by local extension, by lymphatic dissemination to regional pelvic lymph nodes (usually the internal iliac nodes), and hematogenously, especially to the spine. Pelvic lymph node dissection is therefore commonly performed with radical prostatectomy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Superficial inguinal nodes drain the external genitalia and perineal skin, not the prostate.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Para-aortic nodes are not the regional nodal group described for prostate cancer spread.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Left supraclavicular nodal involvement is not the regional pattern of prostatic dissemination.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Mediastinal nodes are distant from the pelvic drainage of the prostate and are not the usual first site.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old man with untreated advanced prostate adenocarcinoma presents unable to void for 18 hours. He has a tender, distended suprapubic mass, and serum creatinine has risen from 1.1 to 3.6 mg/dL. Which of the following best explains his presentation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Narrowing of the urethra by tumor causing urinary retention

choices.label: B
choices.text: Osteoblastic vertebral metastases compressing the spinal cord

choices.label: C
choices.text: Radiation proctitis involving the anterior rectal wall

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mineralocorticoid excess from CYP17 inhibition

choices.label: E
choices.text: Perineural invasion of the pudendal nerve

explanation.summary: Advanced prostate cancer can cause urethral stenosis, leading to urinary retention and renal failure.
explanation.whyCorrect: In advanced cases, prostate cancer causes urethral stenosis, or narrowing of the urethra. This may produce disturbing lower urinary symptoms, and it may progress to significant urinary retention and renal failure, as reflected here by a distended bladder and a sharply rising creatinine.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Cord compression from metastases would produce back pain and neurologic deficits rather than a distended obstructed bladder with rising creatinine.
whyWrongByChoice.C: He has received no radiation therapy, and proctitis causes diarrhea and rectal bleeding, not urinary retention.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mineralocorticoid excess is an adverse effect of abiraterone, causing hypertension, hypokalemia, and edema; this patient is untreated.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Perineural invasion is a histologic feature contributing to local extension, not a cause of acute obstructive retention.

questions.stem: A prostate biopsy core from a 71-year-old man shows sheets of malignant cells with no gland formation and extensive invasion of surrounding tissue. Which of the following Gleason patterns best describes this architecture?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Pattern 1

choices.label: B
choices.text: Pattern 2

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pattern 3

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pattern 4

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pattern 5

explanation.summary: Gleason pattern 5 is sheets of cells with no glands and significant invasion.
explanation.whyCorrect: The Gleason system grades architecture: pattern 1 is normal-appearing cells small and tightly packed in glands, pattern 2 is well-formed glands with more space between cells, pattern 3 is well-formed glands with some cells invading surrounding tissue, pattern 4 is few glands with cells invading surrounding tissue, and pattern 5 is sheets of cells with no glands and significant invasion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Pattern 1 describes normal-appearing cells, small and tightly packed in glands.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Pattern 2 describes well-formed glands with more space between cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pattern 3 describes well-formed glands with some cells invading surrounding tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pattern 4 describes few glands with cells invading surrounding tissue, but glands are still identifiable.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man's biopsy is reported as Gleason 3 + 3 = 6, and the pathologist notes that 6 is effectively the lowest score assigned in contemporary practice even though the system's numeric range begins at 2. Which of the following best explains why lower scores are not reported?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Patterns 1 and 2 are not assigned on biopsy specimens

choices.label: B
choices.text: Scores below 6 are reclassified as benign hyperplasia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Only the highest-grade pattern present is reported

choices.label: D
choices.text: The lowest pattern grade in the system is 3

choices.label: E
choices.text: Scores are reported only after radical prostatectomy

explanation.summary: Although Gleason scores range from 2 to 10, patterns 1 and 2 are not assigned on biopsy, so reported scores effectively run 6 to 10.
explanation.whyCorrect: The Gleason score is formed by adding the two most prevalent architectural patterns, giving a numeric range of 2 to 10. In contemporary pathology practice, however, patterns 1 and 2 are not assigned on biopsy specimens, so reported prostate cancer scores are effectively limited to 6 through 10.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Low Gleason scores still represent carcinoma; they are not reclassified as benign hyperplasia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The score sums the two most prevalent patterns rather than reporting only the highest one.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The system itself defines patterns 1 through 5; patterns 1 and 2 exist but are not assigned on biopsy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Gleason scores are assigned on biopsy specimens, which is how the tumor is graded before treatment is chosen.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man has a PSA of 9.2 ng/mL and a firm, irregular nodule on digital rectal examination. Which of the following is required to establish the diagnosis of prostate cancer?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Repeat PSA measurement in 3 months

choices.label: B
choices.text: Technetium-99m whole-body bone scan

choices.label: C
choices.text: Transrectal ultrasound-guided core biopsy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Free-to-total PSA ratio measurement

choices.label: E
choices.text: CT of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast

explanation.summary: Biopsy is the only way to truly diagnose prostate cancer.
explanation.whyCorrect: When suspicion of prostate cancer is high, transrectal ultrasound-guided core biopsy is performed; this is the only way to truly diagnose the disease. Multiple cores are taken, typically 10 to 12 in standard practice, and the specimens are examined for the histologic features of carcinoma and graded.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Serial PSA values can raise or lower suspicion but never establish a tissue diagnosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A bone scan is used to look for distant metastases in patients with a worrisome clinical stage, not to diagnose the primary tumor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The free-to-total PSA ratio refines interpretation of an elevated PSA but cannot confirm malignancy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: CT assesses for extraprostatic disease during staging and does not provide a histologic diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old man with known benign prostatic hyperplasia has a PSA of 4.8 ng/mL. His physician wants to better judge whether this elevation reflects cancer rather than his benign gland enlargement before recommending biopsy. Which of the following is most appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Calculating the free-to-total PSA ratio

choices.label: B
choices.text: Measuring serum testosterone concentration

choices.label: C
choices.text: Repeating the PSA immediately after prostate massage

choices.label: D
choices.text: Obtaining a technetium bone scan

choices.label: E
choices.text: Measuring serum alkaline phosphatase

explanation.summary: PSA density, PSA velocity, and the free-to-total PSA ratio are used to improve the quality of PSA testing.
explanation.whyCorrect: PSA is not specific for prostate cancer and may be elevated by prostatitis, benign prostatic hyperplasia, urinary retention, and procedures that manipulate the prostate. Multiple methods have been proposed to improve test quality, including PSA density, PSA velocity, and the ratio of free to total PSA.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Serum testosterone is followed during androgen deprivation therapy, not used to refine an elevated screening PSA.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Manipulation of the prostate raises PSA and would make a false-positive elevation more likely, not less.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Bone scans are used to look for distant metastases in established cancer with worrisome clinical stage.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Alkaline phosphatase is not among the described methods for improving the quality of the PSA test.

questions.stem: An asymptomatic 54-year-old man undergoes PSA testing after a discussion of benefits and harms. His PSA is 4.2 ng/mL and digital rectal examination is unremarkable. Using age-specific PSA reference ranges, which of the following is the most accurate interpretation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is within the reference range for his age group

choices.label: B
choices.text: It exceeds the reference range for his age group

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is within the reference range for men aged 40-49 years

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is diagnostic of prostatic adenocarcinoma

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is fully explained by age-related prostatic growth

explanation.summary: The age-specific PSA reference range for men 50-59 years is 0-3.5 ng/mL, so 4.2 ng/mL is elevated for this patient.
explanation.whyCorrect: PSA rises with age even in healthy males because prostate size increases, so reference ranges are age-specific: 0-2.5 ng/mL at 40-49 years, 0-3.5 ng/mL at 50-59 years, 0-4.5 ng/mL at 60-69 years, and 0-6.5 ng/mL at 70-79 years. A PSA of 4.2 ng/mL in a 54-year-old exceeds his 0-3.5 ng/mL range, although it would fall within range for a man in his 60s.

whyWrongByChoice.A: His age-specific range tops out at 3.5 ng/mL, which this value exceeds.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The 40-49 year range is 0-2.5 ng/mL, so 4.2 ng/mL is well above that range as well.
whyWrongByChoice.D: No PSA value is diagnostic of cancer; biopsy is the only way to truly diagnose prostate cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Age-related prostate growth is accounted for by the age-specific range, which this value still exceeds.

questions.stem: A healthy, asymptomatic 58-year-old man presents for preventive care and asks whether he should be checked for prostate cancer. His examination is normal and he has no family history of malignancy. Which of the following is the most appropriate approach to screening?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Routine digital rectal examination as the primary screening test

choices.label: B
choices.text: Shared decision-making about PSA-based screening

choices.label: C
choices.text: Transrectal ultrasound-guided biopsy as the initial screening test

choices.label: D
choices.text: Deferring any screening discussion until urinary symptoms appear

choices.label: E
choices.text: Annual technetium bone scans beginning at age 55

explanation.summary: Guidelines call for shared, individualized decision-making about PSA-based screening rather than reflexive testing.
explanation.whyCorrect: Current American Urological Association guidelines recommend shared decision-making regarding PSA-based screening in appropriate patients, and the USPSTF recommends individualized decision-making about PSA-based screening for men aged 55-69 years after discussion of potential benefits and harms. Digital rectal examination may be used as a complementary assessment in selected patients but is not recommended as a routine primary screening test.

whyWrongByChoice.A: DRE is complementary in selected patients and is not recommended as a routine primary screening test.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Biopsy is reserved for patients in whom suspicion of cancer is already high; it is not a screening test.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Screening aims to detect disease while patients are still asymptomatic, since prostate cancer is usually silent early.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Bone scans assess for distant metastases in established cancer and have no role in routine screening.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man with biopsy-proven prostate adenocarcinoma has additional molecular testing performed on the tumor to help predict how aggressive it is likely to be. Alterations in which of the following are most characteristically associated with prostate adenocarcinoma?

choices.label: A
choices.text: BCR-ABL fusion transcript

choices.label: B
choices.text: HER2 amplification

choices.label: C
choices.text: TMPRSS2 and ERG

choices.label: D
choices.text: EGFR and ALK

choices.label: E
choices.text: KRAS and BRAF

explanation.summary: TMPRSS2 and ETS-family transcription factors such as ERG are the molecular markers associated with prostate adenocarcinoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: Some patients undergo molecular testing to further characterize the tumor, and these markers may predict aggressiveness. The markers associated with prostate adenocarcinoma are transmembrane protease serine 2 (TMPRSS2), a protein-coding gene, and members of the erythroblast transformation-specific (ETS) family of transcription factors, including ERG, ETV1, ETV4, and ETV5.

whyWrongByChoice.A: BCR-ABL is not among the molecular markers described for prostate adenocarcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.B: HER2 amplification is not one of the markers associated with prostate cancer aggressiveness.
whyWrongByChoice.D: EGFR and ALK alterations are not the markers described in prostate adenocarcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: KRAS and BRAF are not among the prostate adenocarcinoma markers used to predict tumor behavior.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man has newly diagnosed prostate adenocarcinoma with a Gleason score of 9 and a PSA of 45 ng/mL. His physician is concerned about disease outside the gland. Which of the following is the most appropriate next study?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Repeat digital rectal examination

choices.label: B
choices.text: Serum testosterone measurement

choices.label: C
choices.text: Technetium bone scan

choices.label: D
choices.text: Repeat biopsy with additional cores

choices.label: E
choices.text: Free-to-total PSA ratio

explanation.summary: Patients with a worrisome clinical stage undergo bone scan or CT to identify nodal and distant metastases.
explanation.whyCorrect: Local disease is initially staged clinically using the results of the DRE, PSA test, and histologic examination. The goal of imaging is to identify nodal and distant metastases, and patients with a worrisome clinical stage may undergo a bone scan or a computed tomographic scan to look for distant disease, which this man's high Gleason score and markedly elevated PSA warrant.

whyWrongByChoice.A: DRE contributes to the initial clinical stage of local disease but cannot detect distant metastases.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Testosterone measurement is used to confirm castrate levels during androgen deprivation therapy, not for staging.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The diagnosis and grade are already established; more cores would not assess for extraprostatic spread.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The free-to-total PSA ratio helps interpret a borderline PSA before biopsy, not stage a proven cancer.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man is scheduled for radical prostatectomy for localized prostate cancer. Before the operation, his urologist refers him to pelvic health physical therapy. Which of the following is the primary goal of this preoperative referral?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Preventing radiation proctitis after definitive treatment

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lowering the PSA level before the operation is performed

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reducing urinary incontinence after the prostatectomy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Preventing the testosterone flare of GnRH agonist therapy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reducing the risk of osteoblastic metastases to the spine

explanation.summary: Preoperative pelvic health physical therapy teaches pelvic floor activation to reduce urinary incontinence after prostatectomy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Urinary incontinence and erectile dysfunction are the characteristic complications of radical prostatectomy. Patients are often referred preoperatively to pelvic health physical therapy to learn pelvic floor muscle activation and strategies that reduce postoperative incontinence; postoperative therapy then supports recovery of continence and sexual function as tissues heal.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Radiation proctitis is an adverse effect of radiotherapy, not of surgery, and is not addressed by pelvic floor training.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Physical therapy does not lower PSA; PSA is followed serially after definitive treatment to detect recurrence.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Testosterone flare is a problem of initiating GnRH agonists and is managed pharmacologically, not with therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pelvic floor training does not influence hematogenous spread or the development of bone metastases.

questions.stem: An 84-year-old man with severe heart failure and an estimated life expectancy of less than 10 years is found to have low-to-intermediate-risk prostate adenocarcinoma. He is asymptomatic, and neither he nor his physician intends to pursue curative therapy. Which of the following management strategies is most appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Active surveillance with serial PSA tests and repeat biopsies

choices.label: B
choices.text: Watchful waiting with palliative treatment if symptoms develop

choices.label: C
choices.text: Radical prostatectomy with pelvic lymph node dissection

choices.label: D
choices.text: External beam radiotherapy delivered with curative intent

choices.label: E
choices.text: Docetaxel chemotherapy with androgen deprivation therapy

explanation.summary: Watchful waiting suits patients with limited life expectancy and low-to-intermediate-risk disease, with palliation if symptoms arise.
explanation.whyCorrect: Watchful waiting means observing the disease at regular follow-up visits with no intent for curative treatment. It is reserved for patients with limited life expectancy (less than 10 years) and low-to-intermediate risk, and palliative treatment is provided if symptoms develop or the disease progresses.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Active surveillance is for patients with good life expectancy who remain candidates for curative treatment and are monitored with repeated PSA tests, DREs, and biopsies.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Radical prostatectomy is definitive therapy with curative intent and is inappropriate when curative treatment is not intended.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Radiotherapy is also a curative-intent option, which this patient's life expectancy and goals do not support.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Docetaxel with androgen deprivation is systemic treatment for advanced or metastatic disease, not asymptomatic low-to-intermediate-risk cancer.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with localized prostate adenocarcinoma elects surgical treatment with curative intent. Which of the following best describes the structures removed during this operation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The prostate and both testes, sparing the seminal vesicles

choices.label: B
choices.text: The prostate and bladder, with creation of a urinary diversion

choices.label: C
choices.text: The prostate and rectum, with creation of an end colostomy

choices.label: D
choices.text: The prostate and seminal vesicles, commonly with pelvic lymph nodes

choices.label: E
choices.text: The prostate and penile urethra, with a perineal urethrostomy

explanation.summary: Radical prostatectomy removes the entire prostate and seminal vesicles, commonly with pelvic lymph node dissection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Radical prostatectomy involves removal of the entire prostate and the seminal vesicles, commonly together with a pelvic lymph node dissection, and may be performed open or by a minimally invasive approach. Complications include erectile dysfunction and urinary incontinence.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bilateral orchiectomy is a form of androgen deprivation, not part of radical prostatectomy, and the seminal vesicles are removed.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The bladder is not removed, and no urinary diversion is created in radical prostatectomy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The rectum is not resected; rectal injury from radiation, not surgery, underlies radiation proctitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The penile urethra is preserved and urinary continuity is restored rather than diverted to the perineum.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man completed external beam radiotherapy for localized prostate cancer 6 months ago and has received no other therapy. He now reports several weeks of loose stools and intermittent bright red rectal bleeding. Which of the following is the most likely cause?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Radiation proctitis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Docetaxel-induced enterocolitis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Rectal metastasis from the prostate primary

choices.label: D
choices.text: Androgen-receptor antagonist hepatotoxicity

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mineralocorticoid excess from abiraterone

explanation.summary: Radiation proctitis is a characteristic adverse effect of prostate radiotherapy, causing diarrhea and rectal bleeding.
explanation.whyCorrect: Radiation for prostate cancer may be delivered externally or by brachytherapy. Important adverse effects include erectile dysfunction, irritative urinary symptoms or hematuria, and radiation proctitis, which may cause diarrhea or rectal bleeding as in this patient.

whyWrongByChoice.B: He has received no chemotherapy; docetaxel is reserved for advanced or metastatic disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Prostate cancer spreads by local extension, lymphatics, and hematogenous routes to bone; rectal metastasis is not the expected cause here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hepatotoxicity from androgen-receptor antagonists would present with liver enzyme abnormalities, and he is not taking these drugs.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Abiraterone causes hypertension, hypokalemia, edema, and hepatotoxicity, and he is not receiving it.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer has extensive thoracic vertebral metastases and early signs of spinal cord compression. His oncologist wants to lower testosterone rapidly while avoiding any transient rise that could worsen the compression. Which of the following is the most appropriate therapy to start?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Leuprolide alone

choices.label: B
choices.text: Goserelin alone

choices.label: C
choices.text: Degarelix

choices.label: D
choices.text: Docetaxel

choices.label: E
choices.text: Bicalutamide alone

explanation.summary: GnRH antagonists such as degarelix lower testosterone rapidly without an initial flare.
explanation.whyCorrect: GnRH antagonists such as degarelix and relugolix directly block pituitary GnRH receptors, rapidly decreasing LH and testosterone without causing an initial testosterone flare. This makes them well suited to patients in whom a flare would be dangerous, such as those with impending spinal cord compression.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Leuprolide is a GnRH agonist that initially stimulates GnRH receptors and produces the very testosterone flare that could worsen cord compression.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Goserelin is also a GnRH agonist and carries the same risk of an initial flare.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Docetaxel is a microtubule-stabilizing chemotherapeutic for advanced disease; it does not lower testosterone.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Bicalutamide blocks androgen receptors but does not lower testicular testosterone to castrate levels.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man receiving an androgen-receptor antagonist for prostate cancer reports 6 weeks of tender enlargement of both breasts. He takes no other new medications. Which of the following laboratory studies is most important to monitor in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Serum potassium

choices.label: B
choices.text: Serum aminotransferases

choices.label: C
choices.text: Serum calcium

choices.label: D
choices.text: Serum creatinine

choices.label: E
choices.text: Complete blood count

explanation.summary: Androgen-receptor antagonists cause hepatotoxicity, gynecomastia, and sexual dysfunction, so liver enzymes are monitored.
explanation.whyCorrect: Androgen-receptor antagonists such as bicalutamide, flutamide, and enzalutamide prevent androgens from activating androgen receptors in prostate cancer cells. Their important adverse effects are hepatotoxicity, gynecomastia, and sexual dysfunction, so aminotransferases should be followed in a patient who has already developed gynecomastia on one of these agents.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hypokalemia is a feature of abiraterone-induced mineralocorticoid excess, not of androgen-receptor blockade.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Calcium disturbance is not among the described adverse effects of androgen-receptor antagonists.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Renal failure in prostate cancer results from obstructive urethral stenosis in advanced disease, not from these drugs.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Marrow suppression is not the characteristic toxicity of androgen-receptor antagonists.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man has received leuprolide for 3 years for recurrent prostate cancer. He reports hot flashes, decreased libido, erectile dysfunction, and a 9-kg weight gain, and dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry now shows osteoporosis. Imaging shows no bone metastases. Which of the following best explains these findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chronic androgen deprivation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cumulative docetaxel toxicity

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mineralocorticoid excess from CYP17 inhibition

choices.label: D
choices.text: Diffuse osteoblastic bone metastases

choices.label: E
choices.text: Radiation-induced urinary irritation

explanation.summary: Prolonged androgen deprivation therapy causes hot flashes, decreased libido, erectile dysfunction, muscle loss, osteoporosis, weight gain, and insulin resistance.
explanation.whyCorrect: Leuprolide is a GnRH agonist that, with continuous administration, desensitizes and downregulates pituitary GnRH receptors and lowers testicular testosterone to castrate levels. Common adverse effects of prolonged androgen deprivation include hot flashes, decreased libido, erectile dysfunction, loss of muscle mass, osteoporosis, weight gain, and insulin resistance.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Docetaxel is a microtubule-stabilizing chemotherapy for advanced disease, and this patient is not described as receiving it.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mineralocorticoid excess from abiraterone produces hypertension, hypokalemia, and edema rather than this hypogonadal picture.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Bone metastases are osteoblastic and typically cause pain; imaging here shows no metastases, and they would not explain hot flashes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Irritative urinary symptoms follow radiotherapy and do not account for osteoporosis, hot flashes, or weight gain.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with newly diagnosed prostate adenocarcinoma confined to the gland asks how likely he is to be alive in 10 years, and how that compares with men whose cancer has already spread. Which of the following best reflects the prognosis of prostate cancer?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 50% at 10 years for localized disease

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 99.5% at 10 years for localized disease

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 19% at 10 years for localized disease

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 99.5% at 10 years for metastatic disease

choices.label: E
choices.text: About 75% at 10 years for metastatic disease

explanation.summary: Localized prostate cancer has a 99.5% 10-year survival rate, while survival falls to about 19% with metastatic disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Prognosis depends on stage. Localized prostate cancer carries an excellent 10-year survival rate of 99.5%, whereas survival falls to about 19% once the disease is metastatic. Relapse correlates with the Gleason score, which is why grading guides risk assessment and treatment choice.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Survival for localized disease is far better than this, approaching 99.5% at 10 years.
whyWrongByChoice.C: About 19% is the survival figure for metastatic disease, not for localized cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Metastatic disease carries a markedly worse outlook, around 19% rather than 99.5%.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Survival with metastatic prostate cancer is approximately 19%, well below this figure.
